Myenteric plexus in the lamina propria 4. Exclusively under the influence of nerves 5. Parasympathetic connects enteric to CNS
questions.stemHtml:
Choose the correct options from the given statements of the enteric nervous system?
1. Vagus is the only afferent from gut
2. Functions independent of brain and SC
3. Myenteric plexus in the lamina propria
4. Exclusively under the influence of nerves
5. Parasympathetic connects enteric to CNS
questions.solution: (ENS) is a self-regulating system that can function independently of the brain and spinal cord (SC) , controlling gut motility, secretion, and blood flow. Vagus is not the only afferent from the gut ; the gut also has spinal afferents that carry pain and reflex information. The myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus) is located between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers , not in the lamina propria . {{caption_text}} Auerbach plexus between two sets of muscles The ENS is influenced by hormones and local factors , not exclusively by nerves. The parasympathetic nervous system (via vagus and pelvic nerves) connects the ENS to the CNS , modulating its activity. Components of the Enteric Nervous System Component Function Location Myenteric Plexus (Auerbach) Controls motility and peristalsis Between muscle layers Submucosal Plexus (Meissner) Regulates secretion and blood flow In submucosa Autonomy Functions independently but modulated by CNS Entire gut wall 1,2,3 (Option A): Incorrect because the vagus is not the only afferent , and the myenteric plexus is not in the lamina propria . 1,4 (Option B): Incorrect because ENS is not exclusively under neural influence ; hormones and local factors also regulate it. 1,3 (Option C): Incorrect because both vagus-only afferent and myenteric plexus location statements are wrong . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
(ENS) is a self-regulating system that can function independently of the brain and spinal cord (SC), controlling gut motility, secretion, and blood flow.
  • Vagus is not the only afferent from the gut; the gut also has spinal afferents that carry pain and reflex information.
  • The myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus) is located between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers, not in the lamina propria.

    • Auerbach plexus between two sets of muscles

    • The ENS is influenced by hormones and local factors, not exclusively by nerves.
    • The parasympathetic nervous system (via vagus and pelvic nerves) connects the ENS to the CNS, modulating its activity.

    Components of the Enteric Nervous System

    Component

    Function

    Location

    Myenteric Plexus (Auerbach)

    Controls motility and peristalsis

    Between muscle layers

    Submucosal Plexus (Meissner)

    Regulates secretion and blood flow

    In submucosa

    Autonomy

    Functions independently but modulated by CNS

    Entire gut wall

    1,2,3 (Option A): Incorrect because the vagus is not the only afferent, and the myenteric plexus is not in the lamina propria.

    1,4 (Option B): Incorrect because ENS is not exclusively under neural influence; hormones and local factors also regulate it.

    1,3 (Option C): Incorrect because both vagus-only afferent and myenteric plexus location statements are wrong.

questions.solutionHtml:
ong>Explanation:

 

  • This MR Angiogram highlights an extracranial artery marked by the arrow, which runs along the lateral aspect of the skull.
  • The superficial temporal artery (STA) is a branch of the external carotid artery, supplying the scalp, temporalis muscle, and forehead.
  • It is commonly seen in angiographic imaging due to its superficial location and prominent branching pattern.

 

Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA)

There are various types of MR angiograms based on different principles and can be classified into non-contrast and contrast enhanced methods.

Non-contrast MRA

Contrast enhanced (CE) MRA

Time-of-flight (TOF) imaging:

  • It is the most prevalent method for Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) in clinical practice.

Phase-contrast MRA:

  • It is more sensitive for identifying slow blood flow and useful for imaging cerebral veins (MR venography or MRV).
  • Effective for detecting dural venous sinus thrombosis and venous stenoses.
  • MRA combined with gadolinium-based contrast agents is called contrast-enhanced (CE) MRA.
     
  • Excellent for quickly visualizing the carotid and vertebral arteries where a large field of view (FOV) is necessary.
     
  • Reduces artifacts caused by turbulent or slow flow.
     
  • Useful for assessing arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), aneurysms, and intracranial stenosis.
  • Two types are:
    • Elliptical-centric
    • Multiphase techniques

questions.stem: IOC for Ureteric calculi is?
questions.stemHtml: IOC for Ureteric calculi is?
questions.solution: Non-contrast CT (NC-CT) KUB is the investigation of choice (IOC) for ureteric calculi due to its high sensitivity (>95%) and specificity (>98%) in detecting even small stones. It provides detailed anatomical visualization without requiring contrast, making it the gold standard for urinary calculi evaluation. Radiographic Investigations: X-ray KUB: Detects 90% of calculi (radiopaque). Radiolucent stones (TIXU): Triamterene, Indinavir, Xanthine, Uric acid. Ultrasound (USG): Screening tool for hydronephrosis and stones in the collecting system. Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP): Early films (1 & 5 min): Assesses contrast excretion & obstructions. Delayed films: Identifies the cause of delayed excretion. Non-contrast Spiral CT (NCCT) – Gold Standard: Most sensitive test for renal/ureteric calculi. Retrograde Pyelogram (RGP): Better anatomical delineation, especially for the distal ureter. Helps detect additional stones & coexisting ureteric diseases (e.g., strictures). USG (Option A): First-line for pregnant women and children, but misses small ureteric stones and lacks sensitivity for ureteral evaluation. CE-CT (Contrast-Enhanced CT) (Option C): Contrast can obscure stones, making it less effective for detecting calculi. Ureteroscopy (Option D): Used for diagnosis and treatment, but not the first-line investigation. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Non-contrast CT (NC-CT) KUB is the investigation of choice (IOC) for ureteric calculi due to its high sensitivity (>95%) and specificity (>98%) in detecting even small stones.
  • It provides detailed anatomical visualization without requiring contrast, making it the gold standard for urinary calculi evaluation.

Radiographic Investigations:

  1. X-ray KUB:
    • Detects 90% of calculi (radiopaque).
    • Radiolucent stones (TIXU): Triamterene, Indinavir, Xanthine, Uric acid.
  2. Ultrasound (USG):
    • Screening tool for hydronephrosis and stones in the collecting system.
  3. Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP):
    • Early films (1 & 5 min): Assesses contrast excretion & obstructions.
    • Delayed films: Identifies the cause of delayed excretion.
  4. Non-contrast Spiral CT (NCCT) – Gold Standard:
    • Most sensitive test for renal/ureteric calculi.
  5. Retrograde Pyelogram (RGP):
    • Better anatomical delineation, especially for the distal ureter.
    • Helps detect additional stones & coexisting ureteric diseases (e.g., strictures).

 

USG (Option A):
First-line for pregnant women and children, but misses small ureteric stones and lacks sensitivity for ureteral evaluation.

 

CE-CT (Contrast-Enhanced CT) (Option C):
Contrast can obscure stones, making it less effective for detecting calculi.

 

Ureteroscopy (Option D):
Used for diagnosis and treatment, but not the first-line investigation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient presents with an inability to bear weight following a trivial trauma. X-rays of the pelvis and thigh reveal lytic lesions with cortical destruction. She has a history of weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old patient presents with an inability to bear weight following a trivial trauma. X-rays of the pelvis and thigh reveal lytic lesions with cortical destruction. She has a history of weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: common cause of lytic bone lesions in elderly patients with a history of weight loss. The femur and pelvis are common sites for metastatic deposits, especially from primary malignancies like breast, lung, prostate, and renal cell carcinoma. Pathological fractures following trivial trauma are characteristic. The X-ray shows focal bony destruction of the acetabulum , causing abnormal joint orientation, but the femoral articular surface remains normal , suggesting a bone lesion rather than joint pathology . Metastatic Tumors to Bone Common Metastatic Tumors Lung carcinoma (male) Breast carcinoma (female) Prostate carcinoma (Osteoblastic) Thyroid carcinoma Clinical Features Known Primary Malignancy: Bone pain (common in spine, ribs, extremities) Pathological fracture (common in spine) Unknown Primary Malignancy: Bone pain leading to destructive lesion diagnosis Pathological fracture due to weakened bone Malignancies Presenting with Silent Primary Thyroid carcinoma Renal cell carcinoma Bladder carcinoma Common Sites of Metastasis Vertebral bodies Ribs Pelvis Humerus Femur Uncommon distal to elbow and knee Eosinophilic Granuloma (Option A): Primarily affects children, commonly involving the skull and vertebral bodies , not typical in elderly patients. Disseminated TB (Option B): Typically involves the hip joint (Tuberculous arthritis) , leading to joint space narrowing and articular surface destruction , which is not seen here . Brown Tumor (Option C): Seen in hyperparathyroidism , with multiple lytic lesions and associated systemic features, which are not mentioned in the case . @Neet_pg_bot

common cause of lytic bone lesions in elderly patients with a history of weight loss.

  • Pathological fractures following trivial trauma are characteristic.
  • The X-ray shows focal bony destruction of the acetabulum, causing abnormal joint orientation, but the femoral articular surface remains normal, suggesting a bone lesion rather than joint pathology.

    Metastatic Tumors to Bone

    Common Metastatic Tumors
    • Lung carcinoma (male)
    • Breast carcinoma (female)
    • Prostate carcinoma (Osteoblastic)
    • Thyroid carcinoma

    Clinical Features
    • Known Primary Malignancy:
      • Bone pain (common in spine, ribs, extremities)
      • Pathological fracture (common in spine)
     
    • Unknown Primary Malignancy:
      • Bone pain leading to destructive lesion diagnosis
      • Pathological fracture due to weakened bone

    Malignancies Presenting with Silent Primary
    • Thyroid carcinoma
    • Renal cell carcinoma
    • Bladder carcinoma

    Common Sites of Metastasis
    • Vertebral bodies
    • Ribs
    • Pelvis
    • Humerus
    • Femur
    • Uncommon distal to elbow and knee

    Disseminated TB (Option B): Typically involves the hip joint (Tuberculous arthritis), leading to joint space narrowing and articular surface destruction, which is not seen here.

     

    Brown Tumor (Option C): Seen in hyperparathyroidism, with multiple lytic lesions and associated systemic features, which are not mentioned in the case.

questions.answerText: Patchy infiltrates are seen in pyogenic pneumonia
questions.solution: data-dictid="d7ccdaffea1692777184e4c19a10aa">community-acquired pyogenic pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus). The most common imaging pattern seen on a chest X-ray for pneumococcal pneumonia is lobar consolidation; meaning a homogeneous consolidation affecting one or more lobes of the lung Patchy infiltrates are not typical for pyogenic pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Classification of Pneumonia Based on Imaging Pattern: Lobar Pneumonia: Unifocal consolidation, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae . In children under 8 years, may appear as “Round Pneumonia” with ill-defined margins. Air bronchograms are common due to patent airways and minimal volume loss. Bronchopneumonia (Lobular Pneumonia): Multifocal distribution, centered around distal airways. Heterogeneous scattered opacities along airway course, coalescing in severe cases. Air bronchogram absent due to airway involvement. Atypical Pneumonia: Features distinct from lobar or bronchopneumonia (discussed in the table below). Causative Agent Specific Imaging Features Streptococcus pneumoniae Most common cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia in adults. Staphylococcus aureus Common in debilitated patients / superinfection in influenza / secondary to IV drug abuse. Cavitation common in later radiographs. Pneumatoceles (seen in children during recovery phase). Klebsiella pneumoniae Occurs in elderly and alcoholics, usually involves the right upper lobe (RUL). Bulging of fissures due to increased involved lung volume. Legionnaire’s disease (Legionella pneumophila) Rapidly spreading pneumonia from contaminated water sources (ACs, coolers, showers). Also presents with diarrhea, mental confusion (hyponatremia), and shock. Actinomycosis Can mimic bronchogenic carcinoma. Soft tissue/bone involvement (periostitis) – key differentiating feature. CT: Peripheral homogeneous consolidation with central low attenuation and pleural thickening (diagnostic feature). Atypical pneumonia (Most common cause: Mycoplasma pneumoniae) Atypical organism (lacks cell walls, resistant to penicillins). Fine reticular/nodular shadows in perihilar region early, which may progress to consolidation (rare lobar involvement). WBC count usually normal. Presents with non-productive cough, absent/minimal sputum. Not aspiration-related. Common in poorly maintained air-conditioned areas. Other viral causes: Influenza A & B, RSV, Adenovirus, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever). Varicella pneumonia Predominantly nodular opacities (5–10 mm). If persistent, may calcify, leading to miliary shadows on CXR. Interstitial infiltrates are seen in Mycoplasma pneumonia (Option B): Mycoplasma pneumonia typically causes atypical pneumonia , with interstitial infiltrates rather than lobar consolidation. Hilar lymphadenopathy with lung infiltrates is seen in malignancy (Option C): Lung cancer, especially small cell carcinoma and lymphoma , commonly presents with hilar lymphadenopathy along with parenchymal lung infiltrates. Aspiration pneumonia is more common in the posterior segment of the upper lobes and superior segment of the lower lobes (Option D): Aspiration pneumonia classically affects the dependent lung segments , particularly the posterior segment of the upper lobes and the superior segment of the lower lobes , especially in supine patients . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
data-dictid="d7ccdaffea1692777184e4c19a10aa">community-acquired pyogenic pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus).
  • The most common imaging pattern seen on a chest X-ray for pneumococcal pneumonia is lobar consolidation; meaning a homogeneous consolidation affecting one or more lobes of the lung
  • Patchy infiltrates are not typical for pyogenic pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

    •  

    Classification of Pneumonia Based on Imaging Pattern:

    1. Lobar Pneumonia:
      • Unifocal consolidation, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
      • In children under 8 years, may appear as “Round Pneumonia” with ill-defined margins.
      • Air bronchograms are common due to patent airways and minimal volume loss.
    2. Bronchopneumonia (Lobular Pneumonia):
      • Multifocal distribution, centered around distal airways.
      • Heterogeneous scattered opacities along airway course, coalescing in severe cases.
      • Air bronchogram absent due to airway involvement.
    3. Atypical Pneumonia:
      • Features distinct from lobar or bronchopneumonia (discussed in the table below).

     

    Causative Agent

    Specific Imaging Features

    Streptococcus pneumoniae

    Most common cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia in adults.

    Staphylococcus aureus
    • Common in debilitated patients / superinfection in influenza / secondary to IV drug abuse.
    • Cavitation common in later radiographs.
    • Pneumatoceles (seen in children during recovery phase).

    Klebsiella pneumoniae
    • Occurs in elderly and alcoholics, usually involves the right upper lobe (RUL).
    • Bulging of fissures due to increased involved lung volume.

    Legionnaire’s disease (Legionella pneumophila)
    • Rapidly spreading pneumonia from contaminated water sources (ACs, coolers, showers).
    • Also presents with diarrhea, mental confusion (hyponatremia), and shock.

    Actinomycosis
    • Can mimic bronchogenic carcinoma.
    • Soft tissue/bone involvement (periostitis) – key differentiating feature.
    • CT: Peripheral homogeneous consolidation with central low attenuation and pleural thickening (diagnostic feature).

    Atypical pneumonia (Most common cause: Mycoplasma pneumoniae)
    • Atypical organism (lacks cell walls, resistant to penicillins).
    • Fine reticular/nodular shadows in perihilar region early, which may progress to consolidation (rare lobar involvement).
    • WBC count usually normal.
    • Presents with non-productive cough, absent/minimal sputum.
    • Not aspiration-related.
    • Common in poorly maintained air-conditioned areas.
    • Other viral causes: Influenza A & B, RSV, Adenovirus, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever).

    Varicella pneumonia
    • Predominantly nodular opacities (5–10 mm).
    • If persistent, may calcify, leading to miliary shadows on CXR.

     

    Interstitial infiltrates are seen in Mycoplasma pneumonia (Option B):

    • Mycoplasma pneumonia typically causes atypical pneumonia, with interstitial infiltrates rather than lobar consolidation.

    Hilar lymphadenopathy with lung infiltrates is seen in malignancy (Option C):

    • Lung cancer, especially small cell carcinoma and lymphoma, commonly presents with hilar lymphadenopathy along with parenchymal lung infiltrates.

    Aspiration pneumonia is more common in the posterior segment of the upper lobes and superior segment of the lower lobes (Option D):

    • Aspiration pneumonia classically affects the dependent lung segments, particularly the posterior segment of the upper lobes and the superior segment of the lower lobes, especially in supine patients.

questions.stem: Not seen in decompression sickness?
questions.stemHtml: Not seen in decompression sickness?
questions.solution: 98b1248373d3">sickness (DCS) is caused by nitrogen bubble formation due to rapid ascent from high-pressure environments. Vision loss can occur due to air embolism affecting the retinal circulation . Hearing loss can result from inner ear barotrauma or vestibulocochlear involvement . Coagulopathy occurs due to vascular injury and activation of coagulation pathways . Hemodilution is not seen in DCS because the condition primarily leads to dehydration , not plasma volume expansion. Pathophysiology of Decompression Sickness System Affected Manifestations Neurological Vision loss, confusion, vertigo, paralysis Otorhinolaryngologic Hearing loss, tinnitus, dizziness Cardiovascular Coagulopathy, gas embolism, shock Pulmonary Dyspnea, chest pain ("chokes") Vision loss (Option A): Incorrect because air embolism can cause retinal artery occlusion . Hearing loss (Option B): Incorrect because inner ear barotrauma and nitrogen bubbles can affect hearing . Coagulopathy (Option D): Incorrect because bubble-induced endothelial damage triggers clotting abnormalities . @Neet_pg_bot

  • Vision loss can occur due to air embolism affecting the retinal circulation.

  • Coagulopathy occurs due to vascular injury and activation of coagulation pathways.

    System Affected

    Otorhinolaryngologic

Pacinian corpuscle (Option C): Incorrect because it detects vibration and not fine touch resolution. All of them (Option D): Incorrect because only Merkel cells contribute to static two-point discrimination , not the others. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An elderly man presents with a 7-month history of progressive dysphagia and bad breath. An image is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An elderly man presents with a 7-month history of progressive dysphagia and bad breath. An image is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ass="customMeta" data-dictid="55052c0f0616927771829c99eec183">barium swallow radiograph showing a posterior outpouching at the pharyngoesophageal junction, characteristic of Zenker's diverticulum. Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal diverticulum that develops due to weakness in the Killian's triangle (between the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and cricopharyngeus muscle). Zenker Diverticulum: False pulsion diverticulum as it protrudes posteriorly above the cricopharyngeal sphincter through the dehiscence of Kilian between the oblique and horizontal fibres of the inferior pharnygeal constrictor. It is due to loss of coordination between pharyngeal contraction and opening of the upper esophagal sphincter. Clinical features When the diverticulum is small, symptoms largely reflect desynchronization of swallowing with pharyngeal dysphagia. As the pouch enlarges: The fundus descends into the mediastinum. Regurgitation of trapped food can occur and lead to aspiration. Main symptom is halitosis and regurgitation. Diagnosis: Barium Swallow Study (Esophagram): To visualize the esophagus and identify the presence of a diverticulum. questions.stem: Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to?
questions.stemHtml: Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to?
questions.solution: trong> (carotid and aortic bodies) primarily respond to low arterial oxygen (PaO₂) . They are activated when PaO₂ falls below 60 mmHg , increasing ventilation to restore oxygen levels. While they also respond to hypercapnia and acidosis , the central chemoreceptors in the medulla are more sensitive to CO₂ and pH changes. Peripheral Chemoreceptors and Their Sensitivity Stimulus Effect on Peripheral Chemoreceptors Hypoxia (↓ PaO₂) Strongest stimulus , leading to increased ventilation. Hypercapnia (↑ PaCO₂) Weak response; central chemoreceptors dominate. Acidosis (↓ pH) Peripheral response occurs, but central chemoreceptors are more significant. Alkalosis (↑ pH) Minimal effect; detected mainly by central chemoreceptors. Hypercapnia (Option A): Incorrect because central chemoreceptors primarily regulate CO₂ levels, while peripheral chemoreceptors have a weaker response. Acidosis (Option C): Incorrect because although peripheral chemoreceptors detect acidosis, central chemoreceptors play a dominant role. Alkalosis (Option D): Incorrect because alkalosis does not significantly stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What causes decrease in GFR?
questions.stemHtml: What causes decrease in GFR?
questions.solution: id="83d76f27051692777202029aee0cd3">filtration rate (GFR) depends on filtration surface area and membrane permeability , both represented by the glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf) . A decrease in Kf occurs due to glomerular damage, thickening of the basement membrane, or mesangial cell contraction , leading to reduced filtration. Conditions like chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetic nephropathy reduce Kf, thereby decreasing GFR . Factors Affecting GFR Factor Effect on GFR Glomerular coefficient (Kf) ↓ Kf → ↓ GFR (e.g., glomerular disease, fibrosis). Glomerular oncotic pressure (πG) ↑ πG → ↓ GFR (e.g., dehydration, increased plasma proteins). Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (PGC) ↑ PGC → ↑ GFR (e.g., hypertension). Bowman’s hydrostatic pressure (PBS) ↑ PBS → ↓ GFR (e.g., urinary obstruction). Decrease in glomerular oncotic pressure (Option B): Incorrect because lower oncotic pressure would increase filtration, thereby increasing GFR . Increase in glomerular hydrostatic pressure (Option C): Incorrect because higher hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus promotes filtration , increasing GFR. Decrease of Bowman's hydrostatic pressure (Option D): Incorrect because a lower Bowman’s capsule pressure would reduce resistance to filtration, leading to an increase in GFR . @Neet_pg_bot

id="83d76f27051692777202029aee0cd3">filtration rate (GFR) depends on filtration surface area and membrane permeability, both represented by the glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf).
  • A decrease in Kf occurs due to glomerular damage, thickening of the basement membrane, or mesangial cell contraction, leading to reduced filtration.
  • Conditions like chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetic nephropathy reduce Kf, thereby decreasing GFR.

    • Factors Affecting GFR

    Factor

    Effect on GFR

    Glomerular coefficient (Kf)

    ↓ Kf → ↓ GFR (e.g., glomerular disease, fibrosis).

    Glomerular oncotic pressure (πG)

    ↑ πG → ↓ GFR (e.g., dehydration, increased plasma proteins).

    Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (PGC)

    ↑ PGC → ↑ GFR (e.g., hypertension).

    Bowman’s hydrostatic pressure (PBS)

    ↑ PBS → ↓ GFR (e.g., urinary obstruction).

    Decrease in glomerular oncotic pressure (Option B): Incorrect because lower oncotic pressure would increase filtration, thereby increasing GFR.

    Increase in glomerular hydrostatic pressure (Option C): Incorrect because higher hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus promotes filtration, increasing GFR.

    Decrease of Bowman's hydrostatic pressure (Option D): Incorrect because a lower Bowman’s capsule pressure would reduce resistance to filtration, leading to an increase in GFR.

options.label: B
options.text: Is lesser than anatomical dead space

questions.solution: ng> (conducting airways) and alveolar dead space (alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused). It occurs when some alveoli receive air but lack sufficient blood flow , leading to inefficient gas exchange . It is calculated using Bohr’s equation , which considers the difference between arterial and expired CO₂ levels . Physiological Dead Space Concept Description Anatomical Dead Space Conducting airways where no gas exchange occurs (e.g., trachea, bronchi). Alveolar Dead Space Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused , contributing to wasted ventilation. Physiological Dead Space Sum of anatomical and alveolar dead space; reflects ineffective ventilation. Can be measured by spirometry (Option A): Incorrect because spirometry measures lung volumes but cannot differentiate dead space ventilation. Is lesser than anatomical dead space (Option B): Incorrect because physiological dead space is always equal to or greater than anatomical dead space. ng> (conducting airways) and alveolar dead space (alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused).
  • It occurs when some alveoli receive air but lack sufficient blood flow, leading to inefficient gas exchange.
  • It is calculated using Bohr’s equation, which considers the difference between arterial and expired CO₂ levels.

    • Physiological Dead Space

    Concept

    Description

    Anatomical Dead Space

    Conducting airways where no gas exchange occurs (e.g., trachea, bronchi).

    Alveolar Dead Space

    Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused, contributing to wasted ventilation.

    Physiological Dead Space

    Sum of anatomical and alveolar dead space; reflects ineffective ventilation.

    Can be measured by spirometry (Option A): Incorrect because spirometry measures lung volumes but cannot differentiate dead space ventilation.

    Is lesser than anatomical dead space (Option B): Incorrect because physiological dead space is always equal to or greater than anatomical dead space.

    Represents inadequately ventilated alveoli (Option C): Incorrect because it is related to perfusion failure, not ventilation failure (which occurs in shunt physiology).

What contributes to the latent period of muscle twitch?
1. Neuromuscular transmission
2. Excitation contraction coupling
3. Reuptake of calcium back into sarcoplasmic reticulum
4. Transmission impulse from nerve
questions.solution: on initiates muscle contraction by releasing acetylcholine (ACh) at the neuromuscular junction. Excitation-contraction coupling propagates the action potential along the T-tubules and triggers Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Transmission impulse from the nerve carries the action potential along the motor neuron to stimulate the muscle. Latent Period of Muscle Twitch Process Role in Latent Period Neuromuscular transmission ACh release at the neuromuscular junction triggers muscle fiber depolarization. Excitation-contraction coupling Action potential spreads through T-tubules, leading to Ca²⁺ release. Nerve impulse transmission Action potential travels along the motor neuron to reach the muscle. 1, 2 (Option A): Incorrect because nerve impulse transmission is a crucial step before neuromuscular transmission and excitation-contraction coupling. 1, 2, 3 (Option B): Incorrect because reuptake of calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum occurs during the relaxation phase, not the latent period. 1, 4 (Option C): Incorrect because excitation-contraction coupling is essential for Ca²⁺ release, and without it, contraction cannot occur. @Neet_pg_bot

on initiates muscle contraction by releasing acetylcholine (ACh) at the neuromuscular junction.
  • Excitation-contraction coupling propagates the action potential along the T-tubules and triggers Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • Transmission impulse from the nerve carries the action potential along the motor neuron to stimulate the muscle.

    • Latent Period of Muscle Twitch

    Process

    Role in Latent Period

    Neuromuscular transmission

    ACh release at the neuromuscular junction triggers muscle fiber depolarization.

    Excitation-contraction coupling

    Action potential spreads through T-tubules, leading to Ca²⁺ release.

    Nerve impulse transmission

    Action potential travels along the motor neuron to reach the muscle.

    1, 2 (Option A): Incorrect because nerve impulse transmission is a crucial step before neuromuscular transmission and excitation-contraction coupling.

    1, 2, 3 (Option B): Incorrect because reuptake of calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum occurs during the relaxation phase, not the latent period.

    1, 4 (Option C): Incorrect because excitation-contraction coupling is essential for Ca²⁺ release, and without it, contraction cannot occur.

questions.solutionHtml:
g>

The clinical scenario of back pain, stiffness, anterior uveitis and sacroiliitis.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) / Marie Strumpell Disease

Definition

Chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the axial skeleton (spine and sacroiliac joints), leading to pain, stiffness, and spinal fusion (bamboo spine).

Etiology

Unknown; genetic (HLA-B27) and environmental factors involved. HLA-B27 is positive in 90% of cases, but not all carriers develop AS.

Pathophysiology

Inflammation at entheses → Erosive changes → New bone formation → Syndesmophytes → Spinal fusion (ankylosis).

Clinical Features

Musculoskeletal Symptoms:

  • Chronic low back pain (worse after inactivity, better with activity)
  • Limited spinal mobility
  • Enthesitis (Achilles, plantar fascia)
  • Peripheral arthritis (hips, shoulders, knees)
 

Extra-articular Symptoms:

  • Ocular: Anterior uveitis (pain, redness, photophobia)
  • Cardiovascular: Aortic regurgitation, conduction issues
  • Pulmonary: Apical fibrosis
  • Gastrointestinal: Associated with IBD

Diagnosis

Based on clinical features, imaging studies, and HLA-B27 gene presence. Modified New York Criteria:

 

Clinical Criteria:

  • Low back pain > 3 months (improves with exercise, not with rest)
  • Limited lumbar spine motion (sagittal/frontal planes)
  • Reduced chest expansion (relative to age/sex)
 

Radiographic Criteria (X-ray):

Bilateral sacroiliitis (grade 2-4) or unilateral sacroiliitis (grade 3-4)

 

Radiological Features:

  • Blurring/haziness of sacroiliac joint

 
  • Juxta-articular sclerosis
  • Vertical/bridging syndesmophytes
  • Squaring of vertebrae

 
  • Bamboo spine

 
  • Trolley track sign
  • Dagger sign

 
  • Shiny corner sign/Romanus lesion (inflammatory lesions at edges of vertebrae)

 

MRI: Early detection of inflammation

 

Clinical Tests:

For Sacroiliitis:

  • Gaenslen’s test
  • Patrick/FABER test
  • Figure of 4 test
  • Pump handle test
 

For Lumbar Spine:

Schober/ Modified Schober test


 

Laboratory Tests
  • HLA-B27 positive (90% of cases)
  • ESR, CRP: Elevated during active disease, but can be normal

Differential Diagnosis
  • Mechanical low back pain
  • Other spondyloarthropathies (e.g., psoriatic arthritis)
  • Degenerative disc disease
  • Fibromyalgia

Treatment

Non-Pharmacological:

  • Physical therapy (mobility/posture exercises)
  • Patient education on disease and exercise importance
 

Pharmacological:

  • NSAIDs (first-line for pain, stiffness)
  • TNF inhibitors (for NSAID-resistant cases)
  • IL-17 inhibitors (Secukinumab)
  • Sulfasalazine (for peripheral arthritis)
  • Corticosteroids (short-term flare control)
 

Surgical:

  • Hip replacement (for severe hip involvement)
  • Spinal surgery (for severe deformities/fractures)

Complications
  • Spinal fractures (minimal trauma)
  • Cardiac issues (aortic regurgitation, conduction defects)
  • Osteoporosis leading to fracture risk

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best study design as per hierarchy of evidence?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the best study design as per hierarchy of evidence?
questions.solution: Hierarchy of Evidence: Meta-analysis ranks at the top of the evidence hierarchy as it synthesizes data from multiple high-quality studies. Combines Results: It pools results from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or observational studies , increasing statistical power and reliability. Best for Decision-Making: Used in evidence-based medicine (EBM) to guide clinical practice by summarizing large amounts of data. Higher Level than RCTs: While RCTs provide strong evidence, a meta-analysis of multiple high-quality RCTs offers even stronger conclusions. Hierarchy of Evidence in Clinical Research In evidence-based medicine , study designs are ranked based on their reliability in guiding clinical decision-making. Level Study Design Strength of Evidence 1a Meta-analysis of RCTs Highest - Combines data from multiple studies for stronger conclusions. 1b Large RCT (Randomized Controlled Trial) Strong - Best for causality, but single studies may have limitations. 2a Cohort Study Moderate - Observational, used for prognosis and risk factor assessment. 2b Case-Control Study Weaker - Retrospective, useful for rare diseases. 3 Cross-sectional & Case Series Weak - Descriptive, no causal inference. 4 Expert Opinion & Case Reports Weakest - No statistical comparison, potential bias. Case control study (Option B): Incorrect because case-control studies are retrospective and prone to bias, ranking lower in the hierarchy. Cohort study (Option C): Incorrect because while prospective cohort studies provide stronger evidence than case-control studies , they are inferior to RCTs and meta-analyses . Large RCT (Option D): Incorrect because while RCTs are the gold standard for individual studies , a meta-analysis of multiple RCTs provides even higher-quality evidence. @Neet_pg_bot

Step

questions.stem: Malaria detection on the field is done by which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: Malaria detection on the field is done by which of the following?
questions.solution: HRP2 antigen-based Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) is the preferred method for malaria detection in field settings due to its quick results (15–20 minutes), ease of use, and minimal technical expertise requirement . RDTs detect Plasmodium falciparum-specific HRP2 antigen or Plasmodium lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH) for all species . Unlike microscopy (thick/thin smear) , RDTs do not require a microscope or trained personnel, making them ideal for remote and resource-limited areas . questions.answerText: Sexual abstinence, using condoms, delaying pregnancy is helpful in controlling the disease
questions.solution: Zika virus spreads primarily through Aedes mosquito bites and sexual transmission. Sexual transmission is well-documented, hence abstinence, condom use, and delaying pregnancy help prevent spread. No FDA-approved vaccine is available for Zika virus prevention. Zika Virus – Epidemiology, Prevention, and Control Overview of Zika Virus Zika virus is a Flavivirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes (A. aegypti and A. albopictus). It causes mild flu-like illness , but severe complications include congenital Zika syndrome (microcephaly) and Guillain-Barré syndrome . Modes of Transmission Mosquito bites – Primary mode of spread. Sexual transmission – Virus persists in semen, vaginal fluids. Maternal-fetal transmission – Can cause congenital defects. Blood transfusion – Rare but possible. Zika Virus – Epidemiology, Prevention, and Control

Overview of Zika Virus

Zika virus is a Flavivirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes (A. aegypti and A. albopictus). It causes mild flu-like illness, but severe complications include congenital Zika syndrome (microcephaly) and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Modes of Transmission

  • Mosquito bites – Primary mode of spread.
  • Sexual transmission – Virus persists in semen, vaginal fluids.
  • Maternal-fetal transmission – Can cause congenital defects.
  • Blood transfusion – Rare but possible.

  • Zika virus is structurally similar to dengue virus, leading to concerns about antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE).

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following vaccines is not recommended after 65 years?
questions.solution: HPV vaccine is not routinely recommended after 26 years and is generally not given after 45 years, as older individuals are less likely to benefit. Influenza, Pneumococcal, and Herpes Zoster vaccines are strongly recommended for adults ≥65 years to prevent severe infections. HPV vaccination is primarily for younger individuals to prevent cervical and other HPV-related cancers. Older adults have likely been exposed to HPV already , reducing vaccine efficacy. questions.stem: ICER is a unit for which of the following economical analysis?
questions.stemHtml: ICER is a unit for which of the following economical analysis?
questions.solution: ICER (Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio) is a key metric used in cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA). ICER is calculated as: ICER= Change in Effectiveness/ Change in Cost​ Cost is measured in monetary units (e.g., dollars). Effectiveness is measured in health outcomes (e.g., life-years gained, reduction in disease incidence). CEA helps policymakers compare healthcare interventions based on cost per unit of health benefit. ICER is commonly used in health economics to decide whether a new treatment is worth its cost. Economic Analysis in Healthcare Health economic evaluations help determine the best use of resources by comparing costs and benefits of different interventions. Type of Analysis Measure Used Unit of Benefit Example Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) ICER Natural health units (e.g., life-years gained, infections prevented) Comparing two drugs for hypertension based on BP reduction Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) Net Monetary Benefit (NMB) Money Assessing whether a vaccination program saves more money than it costs Cost-Utility Analysis (CUA) Cost per QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) Comparing cancer treatments based on survival & quality of life Cost-Minimization Analysis (CMA) Lowest Cost Option No effectiveness measure (assumes equal outcomes) Choosing between two equivalent generic drugs based on price Cost-benefit (Option B): Incorrect because CBA measures outcomes in monetary terms, not effectiveness per cost unit (ICER). Cost-utility (Option C): Incorrect because CUA uses QALY, not ICER, to compare interventions. Cost margin (Option D): Incorrect because "cost margin" is not a standard term in health economic analysis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A student went on a trip to Jaisalmer, where the temp was 40 degrees, and relative humidity was 20%. What will the mechanism of heat loss be?
questions.stemHtml: A student went on a trip to Jaisalmer, where the temp was 40 degrees, and relative humidity was 20%. What will the mechanism of heat loss be?
questions.solution: At high temperatures (40°C), radiation and conduction contribute less to heat loss since the surrounding environment is also hot. Relative humidity is low (20%), which allows for efficient evaporation of sweat from the skin. Evaporation is the most effective cooling mechanism in dry and hot climates, as sweat evaporates quickly, carrying away body heat. Radiation works best when the surrounding environment is cooler than the body, which is not the case here. Conduction requires direct contact with a cooler surface, which is not significant in this scenario. Mechanisms of Heat Loss in the Human Body The body regulates temperature through four primary heat loss mechanisms: Mechanism Description Effectiveness in a Hot, Dry Climate Evaporation Heat loss through sweat evaporation Most effective (low humidity allows efficient sweat evaporation) Radiation Emission of infrared heat waves to cooler surroundings Less effective (ambient temp is high, reducing heat gradient) Conduction Direct heat transfer through contact with a cooler object Minimal (air and objects in the desert are also hot) Convection Heat transfer via air movement Limited (unless there is strong wind aiding heat dissipation) In hot and dry environments like Jaisalmer, evaporation is the dominant mechanism for heat loss, as sweat evaporates efficiently due to low humidity. Radiation (Option B): Incorrect because radiative heat loss is minimal when ambient temperature is high (40°C). Conduction with air (Option C): Incorrect because air is a poor conductor of heat, and in desert conditions, it is already warm. Conduction with objects (Option D): Incorrect because objects like sand and rocks in Jaisalmer absorb heat and are usually hotter than the body. @Neet_pg_bot

Stage

Description

Formation

Acts as a site for epiblast cell migration, which forms the mesoderm and endoderm.

questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy underwent splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura. During the procedure, the surgeon noticed bleeding while separating the spleen from the stomach. Which vessel is most likely implicated in this bleeding?
questions.solution: hort gastric vessels arise from the splenic artery and drain into the splenic vein . These vessels run within the gastrosplenic ligament , connecting the fundus of the stomach to the spleen. During splenectomy , when the spleen is being separated from the stomach, these vessels must be ligated to prevent bleeding. Since the short gastric arteries lack a collateral blood supply , their injury can lead to fundal ischemia . questions.solution: i>HSL (Hormone-Sensitive Lipase): This enzyme is involved in the breakdown of stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol. In a diabetic patient, increased levels of HSL can contribute to higher levels of free fatty acids, which can promote VLDL (Very Low-Density Lipoprotein) synthesis in the liver. LPL (Lipoprotein Lipase): LPL is responsible for the hydrolysis of triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons, converting them into free fatty acids and glycerol. In diabetes, high HSL activity and low LPL activity both contribute to increased levels of VLDL. High HSL promotes the production of triglycerides in the liver, while low LPL reduces the breakdown of these triglycerides in the bloodstream, resulting in elevated VLDL levels. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Rucaparib is a PARP (Poly ADP-Ribose Polymerase) inhibitor used in the treatment of certain types of breast cancer, particularly those with BRCA mutations. Rucaparib: It is an oral PARP1–3 inhibitor approved in 2016 for advanced ovarian cancer with BRCA mutations, used in maintenance after platinum-based chemotherapy. It is also indicated for BRCA-mutated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after endocrine and taxane therapy. It shares safety concerns with olaparib, including risks of MDS and AML . It is primarily metabolized by CYP2D6 and affects the metabolism of drugs like warfarin . The mean half-life is 25.9 hours. PARP inhibitors work by blocking the repair of DNA damage, leading to the death of cancer cells. Olaparib Rucaparib Niraparib Talazoparib Palbociclib (Option B) is a CDK4/6 inhibitor used in the treatment of HR-positive , HER2-negative breast cancer. It does not inhibit PARP and is not used as a PARP inhibitor. Vemurafenib (Option C) is a BRAF inhibitor , specifically targeting BRAF V600E mutations in cancers like melanoma . It does not affect PARP or its associated pathways. Gemcitabine (Option D) is a chemotherapy agent that inhibits DNA synthesis by interfering with nucleotides. It is not a PARP inhibitor and is used to treat various cancers like pancreatic cancer and non-small cell lung cancer . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: /strong> Gemfibrozil is mainly used to treat high triglycerides (Severe Hypertriglyceridemia) and low HDL cholesterol, but it is not the first-line agent for LDL cholesterol reduction in post-MI patients & also the patient has normal triglyceride levels. questions.stem: What is the half-life of digoxin?
questions.stemHtml: What is the half-life of digoxin?
questions.solution: The half-life of digoxin is approximately 36 hours . This means that it takes about 36 hours for the plasma concentration of digoxin to reduce by half in the body. Since digoxin is primarily eliminated by the kidneys (about 80%), the half-life can be prolonged in patients with impaired renal function. Digoxin: Inotropic Action: Increases intracellular Ca²⁺ , improving heart failure and causing arrhythmias in overdose. Utility: Controls ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation (AF) and terminates reentrant arrhythmias, especially in heart failure patients. Adverse Effects: Toxicity: Common due to low therapeutic index. Symptoms include nausea, cognitive disturbances, blurred/yellow vision, and arrhythmias. Arrhythmias: Includes atrial tachycardia with AV block, ventricular bigeminy, bidirectional VT, and AV block. Severe Toxicity: Hyperkalemia, bradyarrhythmias, and potential unresponsiveness to pacing therapy. Half-Life: 36 hours , with renal elimination as the primary route (80%). Drug Interactions: Drugs like amiodarone, quinidine, and diuretics increase the risk of toxicity by altering digoxin clearance or causing electrolyte imbalances. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
ation:
The preferred initial investigation in a patient suspected of having pheochromocytoma is a 24-hour urine collection for metanephrines, as it is a sensitive and specific test for detecting catecholamine-secreting tumours.

Pheochromocytoma

Definition
  • A catecholamine-secreting tumour that arises from the chromaffin cells of the abdominal sympathetic chain/ adrenal medulla
  • Co-exist with neurofibromatosis, VHL syndrome, MEN syndrome

Clinical features
  • Classical triad: Headache (most common), profuse sweating, palpitation and tachycardia
  • Hypertension (sustained or intermittent)
  • Anxiety, panic attacks
  • Hyperglycemia and Hypercalcemia
  • Pallor (due to alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction)
  • Polyuria and polydipsia
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Erythrocytosis
  • Constipation
  • Abdominal pain
  • Weakness
  • Weight Loss

The rule of 10
  • 10% are bilateral
  • 10% are extra-adrenal
  • 10% are malignant
  • 25-33% are inherited
  • Symptomatic patients do not follow the Rule of 10’s

Diagnosis
  • Measurement of the plasma fractionated metanephrines is the most sensitive screening test; hence, the initial investigation is preferred.
  • Increase 24 hour urinary VMA(Vanillyl mandelic acid) and metanephrines (Option D)
  • MRI is the investigation of choice. (Option B ruled out)
  • Biopsy and CT contrast scans are contraindicated in order to avoid hypertensive crises

Treatment
  • Adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice
  • Size<5cm- Laparoscopic adrenalectomy
  • Preop Alpha-blockers should be given
  • Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment


USG-abdomen (Option A) may sometimes be used to assess abdominal masses, it is not the preferred initial investigation for pheochromocytoma, as it may not detect smaller tumours or those located in less accessible areas, such as the adrenal glands or retroperitoneal space.

 

MIBG (Option C) is specialised imaging studies used for further evaluation, especially in metastatic or multifocal cases, and are not used for initial biochemical confirmation after plasma testing.

questions.stem: Which is the most lethal nerve injury during thyroid surgery?
questions.stemHtml: Which is the most lethal nerve injury during thyroid surgery?
questions.solution: i>The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is a crucial structure in thyroid surgery because it innervates the laryngeal muscles , which control vocal cord function. Bilateral complete injury to the RLN is the most lethal nerve injury during thyroid surgery as it can cause paralysis of both vocal cords , leading to stridor, voice changes, breathing difficulties, and, in severe cases, airway obstruction. Unilateral injury is generally less dangerous than bilateral injury because the contralateral vocal cord can compensate to a significant degree. (Options A & C ruled out) The individual may experience hoarseness or aspiration of fluids through the glottis. Partial injury typically does not lead to significant airway compromise. She is diagnosed with ureteric colic secondary to ureteric calculi. What is the most appropriate diagnostic modality in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A middle-aged woman presents with flank pain and dysuria. The pain was temporarily relieved by intravenous analgesics administered at a nearby primary healthcare center. She is diagnosed with ureteric colic secondary to ureteric calculi. What is the most appropriate diagnostic modality in this case?
questions.solution: -dictid="44b07c254816927771855a12777513">computed tomography (NCCT) is considered the gold standard for diagnosing renal stones. NCCT scans provide detailed images of the urinary tract and can identify both radiopaque (visible on X-rays) and radiolucent (not easily visible on X-rays) stones. Investigations for renal stones: Urinalysis This is often the initial investigation performed. It can reveal the presence of blood (hematuria), white blood cells (pyuria), and crystals in the urine, all suggestive of a possible stone. The pH of the urine can also give clues about the type of stone. Kidney, Ureter, and Bladder (KUB) X-ray It can detect some types of stones, particularly calcium-containing stones, which appear opaque on X-rays. Ultrasound (Option C ruled out) It's particularly useful for detecting hydronephrosis (swelling of the kidney due to urine blockage) caused by stones and can be helpful during pregnancy when minimising radiation exposure is important. Intravenous urogram (IVU) It involves injecting a contrast dye into a vein. The dye travels through the bloodstream to the kidneys, where it is filtered and excreted in the urine. X-rays are taken as the dye passes through the urinary tract, outlining the kidneys, ureters, and bladder. This test can reveal blockages in the urinary tract caused by stones. СЕСТ (Option B) is usually not the first choice for stone detection because contrast can obscure small stones . It should be avoided in suspected acute renal colic cases unless there are other indications. Ureteroscopy (Option D) is invasive and typically performed as a therapeutic procedure to remove stones, not as a diagnostic tool. It is used when stone extraction or biopsy is required but not for routine diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: lass="customMeta" data-dictid="988c19e3131692777183b6744d1920">carcinoma typically presents with dysphagia, initially to solids and later to liquids , as the tumour obstructs and narrows the esophagus. Carcinoma Esophagus Types Squamous Cell Carcinoma Adenocarcinoma Risk Factors Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Smoking, Alcohol, Hot beverages, N-nitroso foods, Adenocarcinoma: Obesity, Gastroesophageal reflux, Barrett's esophagus Clinical Features Progressive dysphagia (initially for solids followed by liquids), Anorexia, Weight loss , Odynophagia, and Regurgitation. Advanced symptoms: Hoarseness, Aspiration, Choking, etc. Investigation Endoscopy: Tumor visualisation, Biopsies, Chromoendoscopy, NBI Barium contrast study: Tumor as ulcerated/stenotic lesion Bronchoscopy: Check airway spread Endoscopic & Percutaneous Ultrasonography: EUS for staging tumour (T stage) and para esophageal nodes Percutaneous ultrasound of cervical nodes with FNA CT scan: Distant node assessment FDG-PET scan: Detects nodes/metastases, not for tumour staging Dysphagia of liquids followed by solids (Option A) is more typical of conditions like achalasia cardia , which leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower oesophagus and failure of the lower oesophagal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing. Chest pain (Option C) can occur in esophageal carcinoma; it is less common as an initial presentation compared to dysphagia . Chest pain in esophageal cancer usually occurs in advanced stages or if there is tumour invasion into nearby structures . questions.solutionHtml:
lass="customMeta" data-dictid="988c19e3131692777183b6744d1920">carcinoma typically presents with dysphagia, initially to solids and later to liquids, as the tumour obstructs and narrows the esophagus.

 

Carcinoma Esophagus

Types
  • Squamous Cell Carcinoma
  • Adenocarcinoma

Risk Factors
  • Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Smoking, Alcohol, Hot beverages, N-nitroso foods,
  • Adenocarcinoma: Obesity, Gastroesophageal reflux, Barrett's esophagus

Clinical Features
  • Progressive dysphagia (initially for solids followed by liquids), Anorexia, Weight loss, Odynophagia, and Regurgitation.
  • Advanced symptoms: Hoarseness, Aspiration, Choking, etc.

Investigation
  • Endoscopy: Tumor visualisation, Biopsies, Chromoendoscopy, NBI
  • Barium contrast study: Tumor as ulcerated/stenotic lesion
  • Bronchoscopy: Check airway spread
  • Endoscopic & Percutaneous Ultrasonography:
    • EUS for staging tumour (T stage) and para esophageal nodes Percutaneous ultrasound of cervical nodes with FNA
  • CT scan: Distant node assessment
  • FDG-PET scan: Detects nodes/metastases, not for tumour staging

 

Dysphagia of liquids followed by solids (Option A) is more typical of conditions like achalasia cardia, which leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower oesophagus and failure of the lower oesophagal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing.

Chest pain (Option C) can occur in esophageal carcinoma; it is less common as an initial presentation compared to dysphagia.

  • Chest pain in esophageal cancer usually occurs in advanced stages or if there is tumour invasion into nearby structures.

 

Neck mass (Option D) can occur if the cancer metastasises to the lymph nodes in the neck (e.g., Virchow's node), but this is not the most common initial presentation.

questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old patient with peptic ulcer disease presents with persistent abdominal pain despite treatment at multiple hospitals. He has ulcers in the jejunum and ileum. His gastric pH is &lt;2, and after discontinuing PPIs, his gastrin levels are 10 times higher than normal. What is the likely lesion, and what are the boundaries of the triangle containing it?

options.label: B
options.text: ﻿﻿﻿Insulinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas

options.label: C
options.text: Gastrinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas

options.label: D
options.text: Gastrinoma; triangle formed by only common bile duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas

questions.answerText: Gastrinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
questions.solution: D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas Explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation of persistent peptic ulcers , especially in the jejunal and ileal regions , combined with elevated gastrin levels (even after stopping PPIs) and a gastric pH <2 , is highly suggestive of a gastrinoma . Gastrinomas are tumours that secrete excess gastrin, commonly leading to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome , which causes multiple peptic ulcers due to high gastric acid production. The gastrinoma triangle refers to a specific anatomical region in the pancreas where gastrinomas are most commonly located. (Pissaros triangle) this triangle is bordered by: Junction between cystic duct and CBD (option D ruled out) Junction of the 2nd and 3rd parts of the duodenum (D2-D3 junction) Junction between the head and neck of the pancreas Insulinoma; triangle formed (Option A) : Insulinomas are pancreatic tumours that secrete insulin , not gastrin . They cause hypoglycemia rather than peptic ulcers, so this option doesn’t fit with the patient’s symptoms or diagnostic findings. (Option B ruled out) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas

Explanation:

  • This patient’s clinical presentation of persistent peptic ulcers, especially in the jejunal and ileal regions, combined with elevated gastrin levels (even after stopping PPIs) and a gastric pH <2, is highly suggestive of a gastrinoma.
  • Gastrinomas are tumours that secrete excess gastrin, commonly leading to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which causes multiple peptic ulcers due to high gastric acid production.
  • The gastrinoma triangle refers to a specific anatomical region in the pancreas where gastrinomas are most commonly located. (Pissaros triangle) this triangle is bordered by:
    • Junction between cystic duct and CBD (option D ruled out)
    • Junction of the 2nd and 3rd parts of the duodenum (D2-D3 junction)
    • Junction between the head and neck of the pancreas


 


Insulinoma; triangle formed (Option A):

  • Insulinomas are pancreatic tumours that secrete insulin, not gastrin.
  • They cause hypoglycemia rather than peptic ulcers, so this option doesn’t fit with the patient’s symptoms or diagnostic findings. (Option B ruled out)

questions.stem: An elderly male presents with foul-smelling breath and dysphagia. A barium swallow X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An elderly male presents with foul-smelling breath and dysphagia. A barium swallow X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: >barium swallow film shows a characteristic radiological finding known as a Pharyngeal pouch or Zenker's diverticulum , and the given symptoms also align with this diagnosis. It is an outpouching of the pharyngeal mucosa through a weak area in the posterior pharyngeal wall (Killian's dehiscence), which can trap food and cause bad breath. Zenker's diverticulum Clinical features: Dysphagia is the most prominent feature appears when the pouch gets filled with food and presses on the oesophagus. Gurgling sound is produced on swallowing. Regurgitation at night from undigested food causes cough and aspiration pneumonia. Halitosis (Chronic bad breathing) Malnourished due to dysphagia. Associated hiatus hernia Rarely can a coma develop in long-standing cases of pharyngeal pouches. Diagnosis: Barium swallow provides information regarding the size, location, and character of the mucosal lining. Endoscopy reveals fibrosis and pooling of food in the diverticulum. Treatment: Excision of the pouch and cricopharyngeal myotomy was done through a cervical approach. Dohlman’s procedure: The partition wall between the oesophagus and the pouch is exposed and divided by diathermy through a weerda scope. Endoscopic laser treatment: Partition wall between the oesophagus and the pouch is exposed and divided by CO2 laser using an endoscope. This procedure is known to have fewer recurrences and faster improvement in symptoms. Tracheoesophageal fistula (Option A) usually presents with cough, vomiting, difficulty in breathing , regurgitation and cyanosis. It is often seen in newborns or in patients with a history of oesophagal surgery or cancer. Achalasia cardia (Option B) is a disorder where the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax properly, leading to dysphagia and regurgitation. Barium swallow shows dilated esophagus with a narrowing at the LES (Bird beak appearance/ Pencil tip appearance/ Rat tail appearance). Carcinoma esophagus (Option C) presents with narrowing or strictures in the esophagus due to tumour growth. Whereas a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) is a protrusion from the pharynx @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: angle between the camera port and the working port in laparoscopic surgery. The ideal azimuth angle is between 30 - 45° for maximum productivity. Angles of laparoscopy Azimuth angle It is the angle between the camera port and the working port in laparoscopic surgery; the ideal azimuth angle is between 30 - 45° to avoid clashing of the instruments. Manipulation angle It is the angle between two working ports, and the ideal angle for this is 60°. Elevation angle This term is more related to the vertical positioning of instruments or the camera in relation to the surgical field, not the angle between ports; the ideal angle for this is also 60°. Crossing angle (Option C) is not a term specifically used to describe the angle between the camera port and the working port. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: c than serum amylase Explanation: The most likely diagnosis here is acute pancreatitis , given the acute epigastric pain, fever, history of cholelithiasis, abdominal guarding, rigidity, & elevated serum amylase and lipase levels along with leukocytosis. Serum lipase is indeed more specific than amylase for diagnosing acute pancreatitis. While both enzymes are elevated in pancreatitis, lipase tends to remain elevated longer and is more directly associated with pancreatic damage. (Option A ruled out) Serum amylase levels can also be elevated in other acute abdominal conditions such as perforation, volvulus, and torsion. If amylase remains elevated for more than a few weeks, it could indicate a chronic condition or other non-pancreatic diseases. > 75 per cent of patients present with hypercalcemia (Option B) : Hypercalcemia is not a common feature of acute pancreatitis. In fact, hypocalcemia is more commonly observed in acute pancreatitis, which happens due to the precipitation of calcium salts in the pancreatic tissue because of the saponification of fat. Increase in the level of serum lipase is directly proportional to the severity (Option D) : Lipase and amylase do not directly correlate with the severity of the disease, and n one of the commonly used scoring systems for grading pancreatitis directly rely on the values of amylase or lipase to assess the severity of the condition. @Neet_pg_bot

c than serum amylase

Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis here is acute pancreatitis, given the acute epigastric pain, fever, history of cholelithiasis, abdominal guarding, rigidity, & elevated serum amylase and lipase levels along with leukocytosis.
  • Serum lipase is indeed more specific than amylase for diagnosing acute pancreatitis.
  • While both enzymes are elevated in pancreatitis, lipase tends to remain elevated longer and is more directly associated with pancreatic damage. (Option A ruled out)
  • Serum amylase levels can also be elevated in other acute abdominal conditions such as perforation, volvulus, and torsion.
  • If amylase remains elevated for more than a few weeks, it could indicate a chronic condition or other non-pancreatic diseases.

> 75 per cent of patients present with hypercalcemia (Option B):

  • Hypercalcemia is not a common feature of acute pancreatitis.
  • In fact, hypocalcemia is more commonly observed in acute pancreatitis, which happens due to the precipitation of calcium salts in the pancreatic tissue because of the saponification of fat.

Increase in the level of serum lipase is directly proportional to the severity (Option D):

  • Lipase and amylase do not directly correlate with the severity of the disease, and none of the commonly used scoring systems for grading pancreatitis directly rely on the values of amylase or lipase to assess the severity of the condition.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male had surgery for an ileal perforation. Due to significant contamination, only the sheath was sutured, leaving the wound open. Daily wound irrigation was carried out, and the wound was closed on postoperative day 5. What type of wound-healing mechanism is occurring in this scenario?
questions.solution: type of wound healing mechanism described in this scenario is tertiary intention (also known as ( delayed primary closure ). Wound healing Healing by primary intention (Option A ruled out) It occurs when the edges of a clean wound are brought together and secured with sutures, staples, or adhesives. Minimal scarring occurs. Healing by secondary intention (Option B ruled out) The wound is left open to heal by granulation, contraction, and epithelialisation. This is common in wounds with significant tissue loss or contamination. Healing by tertiary intention (delayed primary closure) (Option C) The wound is initially left open and then closed surgically after several days when it's clean and granulating. This is used for contaminated wounds to prevent infection. Quaternary intention (Option D) is not a recognised term in wound healing. The proper classification includes primary, secondary, and tertiary intention. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A friend of yours is teaching you about enhanced recovery after surgery. Which of the following statements he makes is inaccurate?
questions.stemHtml: A friend of yours is teaching you about enhanced recovery after surgery. Which of the following statements he makes is inaccurate?

options.label: B
options.text: Epidural anaesthesia recommended in laparoscopic surgery for pain control

options.label: C
options.text: Reduction of hospital stay by 2-3 weeks

options.label: D
options.text: Beta-blockers are given after major surgery done under general anaesthesia to improve the outcome

questions.solution: is necessary Explanation: ERAS protocols emphasise reducing fasting times before surgery. It allows a light meal up to six hours before surgery and clear fluids up to two hours prior. It also includes carbohydrate-rich drinks up to two hours before the procedure as it helps reduce postoperative insulin resistance, preserve muscle mass, minimize protein loss, and alleviate preoperative thirst, hunger, and anxiety. ERAS is a set of evidence-based guidelines aimed at improving recovery after surgery. It focuses on optimising preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative care to speed up recovery, reduce complications, and shorten hospital stays. Epidural anaesthesia recommended in laparoscopic surgery for pain control (Option B) is true because it is one of the main component of ERAS and it can be used for effective pain control in many types of surgery, including laparoscopic surgery. However, its use may depend on the type of surgery and the patient’s condition. Reduction of hospital stay by 2-3 weeks (Option C) is correct as one of the key goals of ERAS is to reduce the length of hospital stay. Beta-blockers are given after major surgery done under general anaesthesia to improve outcome (Option D) is true and is mainly given to improve cardiovascular outcome. Reference: @Neet_pg_bot

is necessary

questions.stem: A chronic smoker presents with leg pain after walking 100 meters. On examination, there is an absent pulse in the bilateral dorsalis pedis, anterior tibial, and posterior tibial arteries, but no gangrene is noted. Intermittent claudication is suspected. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?
questions.stemHtml: A chronic smoker presents with leg pain after walking 100 meters. On examination, there is an absent pulse in the bilateral dorsalis pedis, anterior tibial, and posterior tibial arteries, but no gangrene is noted. Intermittent claudication is suspected. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Pain is more at night and sleep

options.label: B
options.text: Pain aggravated by standing and relieved by bending forward

options.label: C
options.text: Development of pain on the 1st step of walking

options.label: D
options.text: Pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest

questions.answerText: Pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest
questions.solution: >This is a classic symptom of peripheral artery disease (PAD) . The pain is typically muscle pain , cramping , or aching , and it most commonly affects the calf muscles because of their large muscle mass and high demand for oxygen during activity. Boyd's classification of intermittent claudication : Grade Description Grade 0: Asymptomatic No symptoms of claudication, even with exercise Grade I: Mild claudication Able to walk more than 200 meters (about 650 feet) before onset of symptoms Grade II: Moderate claudication Able to walk between 50 and 200 meters (about 160 to 650 feet) before onset of symptoms Grade III: Severe claudication Able to walk less than 50 meters (about 160 feet) before onset of symptoms Grade IV: Ischemic rest pain Pain occurs at rest or with minimal exertion Pain is more at night and sleep (Option A) : Night pain is more characteristic of rest pain in advanced PAD, not intermittent claudication. Pain aggravated by standing and relieved by bending forward (Option B) : This description is more consistent with neurogenic claudication and is typical of lumbar canal stenosis , where pain worsens with standing or walking and is relieved by bending forward or sitting. Development of pain on the 1st step of walking (Option C) is associated with osteoarthritis , whereas the pain in intermittent claudication develops after walking for a certain distance, not immediately when taking the first step. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a component of Beck's cognitive theory of depression?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is not a component of Beck's cognitive theory of depression?
questions.solution: Explanation: Introjection refers to the unconscious adoption of the attitudes or behaviours of others, often discussed in the context of psychodynamic theory, not Beck's cognitive theory. Thus, it is not a component of Beck's theory. Psychosocial Theories of Depression: Cognitive Theory Depression arises from cognitive distortions known as depressogenic schemata. Cognitive Triad (by Aaron Beck) : Worthlessness: Negative self-perception. Helplessness: Perception of the environment as hostile and demanding. Hopelessness: Expectation of suffering and failure in the future. Therapy focuses on modifying these cognitive distortions. Life Events and Environmental Stress Stressful life events often precede the first episode of mood disorders. Initial stress may lead to long-lasting biological changes, increasing the risk for future episodes even without further stressors. Psychodynamic Theories Early disturbances in the infant-mother relationship predispose to depression. Depression is linked to real or imagined loss of significant objects. Introjection of lost objects serves as a defense mechanism. Feelings of love and hate toward the lost object result in self-directed anger. Learned Helplessness Developed from studies showing that exposure to uncontrollable stressors (e.g., electric shocks in dogs) leads to passive behaviour. Humans may internalize helplessness and lose self-esteem after adverse events. Improvement in depression involves learning a sense of control and mastery over one’s environment. Evolutionary Theory Depression is viewed as an adaptive response to perceived environmental threats. Withdrawal from social situations and decreased activity may serve as protective mechanisms. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

  • Introjection refers to the unconscious adoption of the attitudes or behaviours of others, often discussed in the context of psychodynamic theory, not Beck's cognitive theory.
  • Thus, it is not a component of Beck's theory.

 

Psychosocial Theories of Depression:

 

Cognitive Theory

  • Depression arises from cognitive distortions known as depressogenic schemata.
  • Cognitive Triad (by Aaron Beck):
    • Worthlessness: Negative self-perception.
    • Helplessness: Perception of the environment as hostile and demanding.
    • Hopelessness: Expectation of suffering and failure in the future.
  • Therapy focuses on modifying these cognitive distortions.

 

Life Events and Environmental Stress

  • Stressful life events often precede the first episode of mood disorders.
  • Initial stress may lead to long-lasting biological changes, increasing the risk for future episodes even without further stressors.

 

Psychodynamic Theories

  • Early disturbances in the infant-mother relationship predispose to depression.
  • Depression is linked to real or imagined loss of significant objects.
  • Introjection of lost objects serves as a defense mechanism.
  • Feelings of love and hate toward the lost object result in self-directed anger.

 

Learned Helplessness

  • Developed from studies showing that exposure to uncontrollable stressors (e.g., electric shocks in dogs) leads to passive behaviour.
  • Humans may internalize helplessness and lose self-esteem after adverse events.
  • Improvement in depression involves learning a sense of control and mastery over one’s environment.

 

Evolutionary Theory

  • Depression is viewed as an adaptive response to perceived environmental threats.
  • Withdrawal from social situations and decreased activity may serve as protective mechanisms.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate treatment for a patient who frequently experiences a sense of contamination in his hands and compulsively washes them, leading to distress and impaired performance?
questions.stemHtml: What is the appropriate treatment for a patient who frequently experiences a sense of contamination in his hands and compulsively washes them, leading to distress and impaired performance?
questions.solution: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) , specifically contamination fears and compulsive washing. The most effective treatment for OCD, especially in cases like this, is Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) . This technique involves exposing the patient to feared situations (e.g., touching something "contaminated") and preventing compulsive behaviour (e.g., hand washing). Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: The patient has recurrent obsessions and compulsions. Recurrent obsessions or compulsions may cause severe distress or anxiety to the person. Obsessions Compulsions Intrusive and unwanted repetitive thoughts, urges, or impulses. Most common: Contamination Repetitive actions or thoughts carried out in a strict, regulation-bound manner or reaction to obsessions Performed to relieve anxiety or fear. Most common: Checking These are time-consuming (at least 1 hr/day) and significantly interfere with the person’s routine, occupational functioning, usual social activities, or relationships. Patients can have only obsessions, only compulsions, or both obsessions and compulsions (most common). The most common comorbidity associated with OCD is major depressive disorder (67%). Major symptom patterns: Contamination / Cleansing Most common presentation. An obsession with contamination followed by washing and avoidance of the presumably contaminated object. Pathological doubt /checking Second most common presentation. Obsession of doubt, usually followed by compulsion of checking. Intrusive/forbidden thoughts Third most common presentation. Obsessed with intrusive thoughts of aggressive or sexual acts without a compulsion. Symmetry/ordering Fourth most common presentation. Patient needs symmetry/precision, which results in the compulsion of slowness. Other symptoms Religious obsessions and compulsive hoarding. Symptom specifiers: Tic related: current or prior history of tic disorder. Patients may have good/fair insight. Patient with poor insight. Patient with absent insight/delusional beliefs. Treatment: Pharmacotherapy: First line: SSRIs (preferred) and Clomipramine Treatment should be continued for 1-2 years Augmenting agents: Antipsychotics: Risperidone, Aripiprazole. Others: Memantine, riluzole, ketamine, lamotrigine, and N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Psychotherapy: Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT): Exposure and response prevention (ERP) Exposure to feared situations is given. The patient is asked not to engage in a compulsive response. Other therapies are desensitization, thought-stopping, flooding, aversive conditioning, psychodynamic psychotherapy, and family therapy. In younger patients , cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is preferred first. In more severe symptoms or comorbid depression, pharmacotherapy is preferred first. A combination of CBT and pharmacotherapy is particularly useful. Somatic Therapies: Anterior cingulotomy and capsulotomy. Deep brain stimulation with implantation of electrodes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Most common hearing test done in neonates for screening:
questions.stemHtml: Most common hearing test done in neonates for screening:
questions.solution: OAE is the preferred screening test in neonates due to its ease of use, reliability, and non-invasiveness. Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) : is a test in which emissions are generated by outer hair cells and are used to evaluate hearing in individuals with cognitive impairments. OAEs are low-intensity sounds produced by the outer hair cells of a normal cochlea and can be elicited by a sensitive microphone placed in the external ear canal. Pathway: The absence of OAE indicates damage in the outer hair cell (conditions like lesions of the cochlea, middle ear disorders, etc.). Types: Spontaneous OAEs involve emissions without any external stimulation (sound). They may be absent in 50% of the individuals. Evoked OAEs require an external stimulus. Transient evoked OAEs (TEOAEs) : Evoked by clicks (mixture of various frequencies). Distortion product OAEs: Two tones (specific frequencies) are simultaneously presented to the cochlea to produce distortion products. Uses of OAE: They are used as a screening test for neonates, uncooperative or mentally challenged individuals. Differentiate between cochlear and retrocochlear hearing loss. Helpful in early detection of noise-induced hearing loss. Clap & Smile (Option A): This is an informal behavioral response test that is subjective and unreliable for neonatal hearing screening. BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) (Option B): This is used for diagnostic confirmation in high-risk infants (ICU) but is not the first-line screening test due to its higher cost and complexity. PTA (Pure Tone Audiometry) (Option D): This requires active patient participation, which is not possible in neonates. @Neet_pg_bot
