questions.solution: LJ medium used to grow tuberculosis. TB lab investigations: Investigations Purpose Advantages Limitations Sputum smear Initial screening for pulmonary TB. Samples are stained using the Ziehl-Neelsen method or Auramine-O stain to visualize acid-fast bacilli (AFB) under a microscope. Quick and inexpensive. Can provide results within a few hours. Low sensitivity, especially in cases of extrapulmonary TB or in patients with HIV. Cannot differentiate between Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM). Culture Methods Confirm the diagnosis of TB and assess drug susceptibility. Solid Media: Sputum is inoculated onto solid culture media like Löwenstein-Jensen or Middlebrook agar. Liquid Media: Automated systems like BACTEC or MGIT are used to detect growth faster. The gold standard for TB diagnosis. Allows for drug susceptibility testing. Time-consuming; results can take weeks. Requires specialized laboratory facilities. Xpert MTB/RIF Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance. Method : A cartridge-based system that performs nucleic acid amplification (NAAT). Sputum or other specimens are processed directly in the cartridge. Rapid results (within 2 hours). High sensitivity and specificity. Simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance. More expensive than smear microscopy. Does not provide full drug susceptibility testing. LAMP (Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification) Detects DNA of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Method : Amplifies DNA at a constant temperature without the need for thermal cycling. Sputum or other specimens are used. Rapid results (within 1-2 hours). High specificity and sensitivity. Can be performed at the point of care. Used for patients with HIV with CD4+ counts of less than 100 cells/μL irrespective of signs and symptoms of TB. Less widely available than PCR-based tests. Cannot detect drug resistance directly. TrueNat Point-of-care test for TB detection. Method : Uses a micro-PCR technology to amplify DNA. Results are available within 60 minutes. Portable and easy to use in peripheral health facilities. Provides results quickly, facilitating immediate treatment decisions. Line Probe Assay (LPA) Detects TB and drug resistance (rifampicin and isoniazid). Method : Sputum samples are processed, and DNA is extracted. Amplified DNA is hybridized to specific probes on a membrane strip. Rapid results (within 1-2 days). Can detect multiple mutations associated with drug resistance. Requires a laboratory setup and trained personnel. Not suitable for all strains of TB. RFLP IS6110 restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis is widely used for molecular epidemiological studies of tuberculosis. Restriction enzymes Nru I, EcoN I, Pst I, and Pvu II were used to analyze IS6110 fingerprints in Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains H37Rv (virulent) and H37Ra (avirulent). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
LJ medium used to grow tuberculosis.

 

TB lab investigations:

Investigations

Purpose

Advantages

Limitations

Sputum smear

  • Initial screening for pulmonary TB.
  • Samples are stained using the Ziehl-Neelsen method or Auramine-O stain to visualize acid-fast bacilli (AFB) under a microscope.
  • Quick and inexpensive. Can provide results within a few hours.
  • Low sensitivity, especially in cases of extrapulmonary TB or in patients with HIV.
  • Cannot differentiate between Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM).

Culture Methods
  • Confirm the diagnosis of TB and assess drug susceptibility.
  • Solid Media: Sputum is inoculated onto solid culture media like Löwenstein-Jensen or Middlebrook agar.
  • Liquid Media: Automated systems like BACTEC or MGIT are used to detect growth faster.
  • The gold standard for TB diagnosis.
  • Allows for drug susceptibility testing.
  • Time-consuming; results can take weeks.
  • Requires specialized laboratory facilities.

Xpert MTB/RIF
  • Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance.
  • Method:
  • A cartridge-based system that performs nucleic acid amplification (NAAT).
  • Sputum or other specimens are processed directly in the cartridge.
  • Rapid results (within 2 hours).
  • High sensitivity and specificity.
  • Simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance.
  • More expensive than smear microscopy.
  • Does not provide full drug susceptibility testing.

LAMP (Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification)
  • Detects DNA of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • Method:
  • Amplifies DNA at a constant temperature without the need for thermal cycling.
  • Sputum or other specimens are used.
  • Rapid results (within 1-2 hours).
  • High specificity and sensitivity.
  • Can be performed at the point of care.
  • Used for patients with HIV with CD4+ counts of less than 100 cells/μL irrespective of signs and symptoms of TB.
  • Less widely available than PCR-based tests.
  • Cannot detect drug resistance directly.

TrueNat
  • Point-of-care test for TB detection.
  • Method:
  • Uses a micro-PCR technology to amplify DNA.
  • Results are available within 60 minutes.
  • Portable and easy to use in peripheral health facilities.
  • Provides results quickly, facilitating immediate treatment decisions.
  

Line Probe Assay (LPA)
  • Detects TB and drug resistance (rifampicin and isoniazid).
  • Method:
    • Sputum samples are processed, and DNA is extracted.
    • Amplified DNA is hybridized to specific probes on a membrane strip.
  • Rapid results (within 1-2 days).
  • Can detect multiple mutations associated with drug resistance.
  • Requires a laboratory setup and trained personnel.
  • Not suitable for all strains of TB.

RFLP
  • IS6110 restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis is widely used for molecular epidemiological studies of tuberculosis.
  • Restriction enzymes Nru I, EcoN I, Pst I, and Pvu II were used to analyze IS6110 fingerprints in Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains H37Rv (virulent) and H37Ra (avirulent).

questions.stem: All of the following are cold sterilization methods except?
questions.stemHtml: All of the following are cold sterilization methods except?
questions.solution: Autoclave is heat sterilization of 121•*15min*15psi. An autoclave is a sterilisation technique that uses moist heat at a temperature > 100 o C. The autoclave (steam steriliser) works on the principle of steam production under pressure. When this steam meets a cooler surface, it condenses, transferring its heat to that surface. The process continues until the surface temperature matches that of the steam. The resulting condensed water provides moist heat, effectively killing microbes on the materials by protein denaturation. Its temperature settings are 121 o C for 15 minutes at 15 psi pressure. Materials that can be sterilised include linen, surgical instruments(non-sharps only), laboratory ware, pharmaceuticals, suture material except catgut(cold sterilisation) and culture media except egg and serum containing media(inspissation). Sterilisation control indicator - Geobacillus stearothermophilus Types of Autoclaves in Healthcare: Laboratory autoclaves Hospital dressing sterilisers Instrument sterilisers Rapid cooling sterilisers @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: DOC for fasciola hepatica?
questions.stemHtml: DOC for fasciola hepatica?
questions.solution: Triclabendazole is DOC for fasciola hepatica. Fasciola hepatica Fasciola hepatica, commonly known as the liver fluke, is a parasitic trematode (flatworm) that primarily infects the livers of various mammals, including humans. It causes the disease fascioliasis, leading to liver damage, biliary obstruction, and inflammatory reactions. Morphology Adult Fluke: Shape: Leaf-shaped, flat, and broad. Size: Approximately 2-3 cm in length and 1 cm in width. Color: Typically brown or grey. Distinctive Features: Cone-shaped anterior end. Two suckers, an oral sucker at the front and a ventral sucker close to it, used for attachment to host tissues. The fluke’s body is covered by a tegument (a protective outer layer) with spines aiding in attachment. Eggs: Size: Large, oval, and approximately 130-150 µm in length. Color: Yellowish-brown. Characteristics: Each egg has an operculum (a lid-like structure) at one end, which opens to release the miracidium (the larval stage). Eggs are unembryonated when passed out in feces. Life Cycle Eggs in Water Eggs are expelled in the feces of infected mammals (definitive hosts). Under suitable environmental conditions, miracidia are released from eggs after 9–15 days. Infection of Snails (Intermediate Host) Miracidia penetrate specific freshwater snails, such as Lymnaea spp. Inside the snail, they progress through stages: sporocyst, redia, and eventually cercaria. Release and Encystment Cercariae exit the snail and encyst on aquatic vegetation, transforming into metacercariae, the infective stage. Infection of Mammals (Definitive Host) Mammals, including humans, become infected by consuming contaminated water or vegetation with metacercariae. In the duodenum, metacercariae excyst, penetrate the intestinal wall, migrate to the liver, and lodge in the bile ducts, maturing into adult flukes. Clinical Presentation Acute Phase (Invasive or Hepatic Stage): Duration: Begins about 2-3 weeks post-infection and may last for several months. Symptoms: Fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), and occasionally jaundice. Nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Eosinophilia (elevated eosinophil count in blood). Chronic Phase (Biliary Stage): Duration: Occurs months to years post-infection. Symptoms: Biliary colic, obstructive jaundice, and cholangitis (inflammation of the bile ducts). Gallbladder symptoms, liver abscesses, and secondary bacterial infections in severe cases. Possible fibrosis of the bile ducts with prolonged infection. Investigations Serology: ELISA for detection of anti-Fasciola antibodies (sensitive in both acute and chronic infections). Immunoblotting can also confirm the diagnosis. Stool Examination: Microscopic detection of eggs in stool samples; however, eggs are typically not present in the acute phase and may be difficult to detect in chronic cases. Imaging: Ultrasound: Useful in detecting hepatobiliary abnormalities such as bile duct dilation or liver abscesses. CT/MRI: May show liver lesions or track the migration of larvae in the liver. Blood Tests: Eosinophilia is common in the acute phase. Liver function tests: Elevated liver enzymes, especially in chronic disease. Management Antiparasitic Treatment: Triclabendazole: The drug of choice, effective against both adult and larval stages. Dosage: Oral dose of 10-12 mg/kg, with a repeat dose after 12 hours if needed. Alternative Medications: Bithionol: Sometimes used if triclabendazole is unavailable. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Triclabendazole is DOC for fasciola hepatica.

 

Fasciola hepatica


Fasciola hepatica, commonly known as the liver fluke, is a parasitic trematode (flatworm) that primarily infects the livers of various mammals, including humans. It causes the disease fascioliasis, leading to liver damage, biliary obstruction, and inflammatory reactions.

 

Morphology

Adult Fluke:

 

 

  • Shape: Leaf-shaped, flat, and broad.
  • Size: Approximately 2-3 cm in length and 1 cm in width.
  • Color: Typically brown or grey.
  • Distinctive Features:
    • Cone-shaped anterior end.
    • Two suckers, an oral sucker at the front and a ventral sucker close to it, used for attachment to host tissues.
    • The fluke’s body is covered by a tegument (a protective outer layer) with spines aiding in attachment.

 

Eggs:

 

 

  • Size: Large, oval, and approximately 130-150 µm in length.
  • Color: Yellowish-brown.
  • Characteristics:
    • Each egg has an operculum (a lid-like structure) at one end, which opens to release the miracidium (the larval stage).
    • Eggs are unembryonated when passed out in feces.

 

Life Cycle

 

 

  1. Eggs in Water
  • Eggs are expelled in the feces of infected mammals (definitive hosts).
  • Under suitable environmental conditions, miracidia are released from eggs after 9–15 days.
  1. Infection of Snails (Intermediate Host)
  • Miracidia penetrate specific freshwater snails, such as Lymnaea spp.
  • Inside the snail, they progress through stages: sporocyst, redia, and eventually cercaria.
  1. Release and Encystment
  • Cercariae exit the snail and encyst on aquatic vegetation, transforming into metacercariae, the infective stage.
  1. Infection of Mammals (Definitive Host)
  • Mammals, including humans, become infected by consuming contaminated water or vegetation with metacercariae.
  • In the duodenum, metacercariae excyst, penetrate the intestinal wall, migrate to the liver, and lodge in the bile ducts, maturing into adult flukes.

 

Clinical Presentation

Acute Phase (Invasive or Hepatic Stage):

  • Duration: Begins about 2-3 weeks post-infection and may last for several months.
  • Symptoms:
    • Fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
    • Hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), and occasionally jaundice.
    • Nausea, vomiting, and weight loss.
    • Eosinophilia (elevated eosinophil count in blood).

Chronic Phase (Biliary Stage):

  • Duration: Occurs months to years post-infection.
  • Symptoms:
    • Biliary colic, obstructive jaundice, and cholangitis (inflammation of the bile ducts).
    • Gallbladder symptoms, liver abscesses, and secondary bacterial infections in severe cases.
    • Possible fibrosis of the bile ducts with prolonged infection.

 

Investigations

  1. Serology:
    • ELISA for detection of anti-Fasciola antibodies (sensitive in both acute and chronic infections).
    • Immunoblotting can also confirm the diagnosis.
  2. Stool Examination:
    • Microscopic detection of eggs in stool samples; however, eggs are typically not present in the acute phase and may be difficult to detect in chronic cases.
  3. Imaging:
    • Ultrasound: Useful in detecting hepatobiliary abnormalities such as bile duct dilation or liver abscesses.
    • CT/MRI: May show liver lesions or track the migration of larvae in the liver.
  4. Blood Tests:
    • Eosinophilia is common in the acute phase.
    • Liver function tests: Elevated liver enzymes, especially in chronic disease.

 

Management

Antiparasitic Treatment:

  • Triclabendazole: The drug of choice, effective against both adult and larval stages. Dosage: Oral dose of 10-12 mg/kg, with a repeat dose after 12 hours if needed.

Alternative Medications:

  • Bithionol: Sometimes used if triclabendazole is unavailable.

questions.solution: Cryptococcus occurs when CD4<350 The India ink stain (A type of negative stain) is specifically used to visualize the capsule surrounding Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF samples. A clear halo around the yeast cells indicates the presence of the capsule, which is an important virulence factor. Urease test positive Maltese cross appearance under polarising microscope Cryptococcus Spp. Cryptococcus is a true yeast. Capsule Polysaccharide capsule - helps in serotyping and protection against phagocytosis . Serotypes A, D, AD serotypes - Cryptococcus variety neoformans B, C serotypes -Cryptococcus variety gattii Virulence factors Polysaccharide Capsule : The primary virulence factor. It helps the pathogen evade phagocytosis and suppresses the host’s local immune responses, enabling the organism to survive and spread. Melanin Production : Cryptococcus produces melanin via the enzyme phenol oxidase, which contributes to its virulence by protecting the pathogen from oxidative stress and immune defenses. Enzyme Production : The fungus secretes several enzymes, including: Phospholipase : Aids in tissue invasion and damage. Urease : Helps the fungus survive in the host environment by neutralizing acidic conditions, enhancing its ability to colonize and spread. Risk of infection Immunocompromised States: HIV/AIDS, cancer, organ transplant recipients, those on immunosuppressive therapies, extremes of age are at higher risk. Geographic Location: Exposure to environments where Cryptococcus gattii is endemic, such as tropical and subtropical regions Environmental Exposure: Exposure to bird droppings or decaying wood can increase the likelihood of infection, especially with C. neoformans. Management of cryptococcosis Microscopy India ink - Demonstrates the capsule, which appears as clear space surrounding the round budding yeast cells Mucicarmine stain: It stains the carminophilic cell wall of C. neoformans Culture Sabouraud Dextrose Agar , forming smooth, mucoid, cream-coloured colonies. Niger seed agar and bird seed agar : Demonstrates melanin production (brown colored colonies) due to phenol oxidase/laccase enzyme. The ability to grow at 37°C and hydrolyse urea differentiates C. neoformans from non-pathogenic cryptococci Antigen detection tests Demonstration of the capsular antigen by Precipitation and Latex agglutination test Treatment Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status. Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes. Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Cryptococcus occurs when CD4<350

 

 

  • The India ink stain (A type of negative stain) is specifically used to visualize the capsule surrounding Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF samples.
  • A clear halo around the yeast cells indicates the presence of the capsule, which is an important virulence factor.
  • Urease test positive
  • Maltese cross appearance under polarising microscope

  • Cryptococcus Spp.

    Cryptococcus is a true yeast.

    Capsule

    Polysaccharide capsule - helps in serotyping and protection against phagocytosis .

    Serotypes

    A, D, AD serotypes - Cryptococcus variety neoformans

    B, C serotypes -Cryptococcus variety gattii

    Virulence factors
    • Polysaccharide Capsule: The primary virulence factor. It helps the pathogen evade phagocytosis and suppresses the host’s local immune responses, enabling the organism to survive and spread.
    • Melanin Production: Cryptococcus produces melanin via the enzyme phenol oxidase, which contributes to its virulence by protecting the pathogen from oxidative stress and immune defenses.
    • Enzyme Production: The fungus secretes several enzymes, including:
    • Phospholipase: Aids in tissue invasion and damage.
    • Urease: Helps the fungus survive in the host environment by neutralizing acidic conditions, enhancing its ability to colonize and spread.

    Risk of infection

    Immunocompromised States:

    • HIV/AIDS, cancer, organ transplant recipients, those on immunosuppressive therapies, extremes of age are at higher risk.

    Geographic Location:

    • Exposure to environments where Cryptococcus gattii is endemic, such as tropical and subtropical regions

    Environmental Exposure:

    • Exposure to bird droppings or decaying wood can increase the likelihood of infection, especially with C. neoformans.
     

    Management of cryptococcosis

    Microscopy

    • India ink- Demonstrates the capsule, which appears as clear space surrounding the round budding yeast cells
    • Mucicarmine stain: It stains the carminophilic cell wall of C. neoformans

    Culture
    • Sabouraud Dextrose Agar, forming smooth, mucoid, cream-coloured colonies.
    • Niger seed agar and bird seed agar: Demonstrates melanin production (brown colored colonies) due to phenol oxidase/laccase enzyme.
    • The ability to grow at 37°C and hydrolyse urea differentiates C. neoformans from non-pathogenic cryptococci

     

    Antigen detection tests

    Demonstration of the capsular antigen by Precipitation and Latex agglutination test

    Treatment

    • Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine
    • Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status.
    • Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes.
    • Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk.

questions.stem: CD4 T-cell activation is done by?
questions.stemHtml: CD4 T-cell activation is done by?
questions.solution: CD4 T-cell activation is done by MHC II. Feature MHC Class I MHC Class II Expression Found on almost all nucleated cells Found mainly on antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and B-cells Antigen Source Presents intracellular antigens (e.g., viral or tumor proteins) Presents extracellular antigens (e.g., bacterial peptides) Interacts With CD8+ T-cells (cytotoxic T-cells) CD4+ T-cells (helper T-cells) Main HLA Genes HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, HLA-DR Structure Consists of one α (heavy) chain and β2-microglobulin; peptide-binding groove formed by α1 and α2 Consists of α and β chains; peptide-binding groove formed by α1 and β1 domains Function Identifies and helps eliminate infected or malignant cells by presenting endogenous antigens to CD8+ T-cells Activates immune response by presenting exogenous antigens to CD4+ T-cells Peptide Length Presents shorter peptides (8-10 amino acids) Presents longer peptides (10-30 amino acids) The antigen is presented by MHC Class I molecules to CD8+ T-cells, leading to cytotoxic T-cell-mediated destruction (Option A): MHC Class I molecules present intracellular antigens to CD8+ T-cells , not CD4+ T-cells. MHC I is not primarily involved in antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases like myasthenia gravis, which involve MHC Class II. MHC Class I molecules are found only on professional antigen-presenting cells, which present the antigen to helper T-cells (Option C): MHC Class I molecules are found on all nucleated cells, not just APCs. Additionally, MHC I interacts with CD8+ T-cells rather than helper T-cells (CD4+). The statement here mischaracterizes both the distribution and the function of MHC Class I molecules. MHC Class II molecules are present on all nucleated cells and help in presenting intracellular antigens (Option D): MHC Class II is restricted to antigen-presenting cells, not all nucleated cells, and presents extracellular antigens, not intracellular ones. In autoimmune reactions, extracellular antigens are generally presented by MHC II to CD4+ T-cells, which is key to the autoantibody production pathway in myasthenia gravis. @Neet_pg_bot

CD4 T-cell activation is done by MHC II.

 

Feature

MHC Class I

MHC Class II

Expression

Found on almost all nucleated cells

Found mainly on antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and B-cells

Antigen Source

Presents intracellular antigens (e.g., viral or tumor proteins)

Presents extracellular antigens (e.g., bacterial peptides)

Interacts With

CD8+ T-cells (cytotoxic T-cells)

CD4+ T-cells (helper T-cells)

Main HLA Genes

HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C

HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, HLA-DR

Structure

Consists of one α (heavy) chain and β2-microglobulin;

peptide-binding groove formed by α1 and α2

Consists of α and β chains; peptide-binding groove formed by α1 and β1 domains

Function

Identifies and helps eliminate infected or malignant cells by presenting endogenous antigens to CD8+ T-cells

Activates immune response by presenting exogenous antigens to CD4+ T-cells

Peptide Length

Presents shorter peptides (8-10 amino acids)

Presents longer peptides (10-30 amino acids)

 

The antigen is presented by MHC Class I molecules to CD8+ T-cells, leading to cytotoxic T-cell-mediated destruction (Option A): MHC Class I molecules present intracellular antigens to CD8+ T-cells, not CD4+ T-cells. MHC I is not primarily involved in antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases like myasthenia gravis, which involve MHC Class II.

 

MHC Class I molecules are found only on professional antigen-presenting cells, which present the antigen to helper T-cells (Option C): MHC Class I molecules are found on all nucleated cells, not just APCs. Additionally, MHC I interacts with CD8+ T-cells rather than helper T-cells (CD4+). The statement here mischaracterizes both the distribution and the function of MHC Class I molecules.

 

MHC Class II molecules are present on all nucleated cells and help in presenting intracellular antigens (Option D): MHC Class II is restricted to antigen-presenting cells, not all nucleated cells, and presents extracellular antigens, not intracellular ones. In autoimmune reactions, extracellular antigens are generally presented by MHC II to CD4+ T-cells, which is key to the autoantibody production pathway in myasthenia gravis.

This method allows direct visualisation of malaria parasites within red blood cells, providing information about the species, parasite density, and stage of development. It is highly specific and widely used, especially in resource-limited settings. It can be used for the detection of malarial parasites as low as 20 parasites / μL Thin smear - for determination of plasmodium species Stains used - Romanowsky stain ( Leishman, Giemsa or JSB stain) Quantitative buffy coat test RBCs with parasites are less dense; thus, concentrate just below the buffy coat of WBC on top of the RBC column Acridine orange is used to induce fluorescence on the parasite, giving a fluorescent greenish-yellow appearance on a red background Microscopic examination of a smear made using the buffy coat is done. Kawamoto fluorescence microscopy Fluorescent dye like acridine orange or benzothiocarboxy purine is used to stain the parasite inside the RBC Parasite DNA is stained fluorescent green, and cytosol RNA is stained red The slide is examined under the fluorescent microscope Used for mass screening in field laboratory Rapid antigen detection test Immunochromatography is done using monoclonal antibody directed against the parasite antigen Parasite F test Monoclonal antibody is used to detect histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2), which is produced by asexual stages of plasmodium falciparum High sensitivity and specificity Can detect low parasitemia (40 parasite / μL of blood) Can detect only the asexual stage of plasmodium falciparum Dual antigen test Detects Parasite lactate dehydrogenase ( pLDH ) and Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein ( PfHRP-2 ) pLDH is produced by trophozoites and gametocytes of all plasmodium spp . questions.solutionHtml:
Hrp 2/Card test is quick and easy test which is used as field test for malaria.

 

  • The gold standard test used for the diagnosis of malaria is microscopy using the Romanowsky stain.
  • This method allows direct visualisation of malaria parasites within red blood cells, providing information about the species, parasite density, and stage of development.
  • It is highly specific and widely used, especially in resource-limited settings.

 

LAB DIAGNOSIS OF MALARIA

Microscopy (Gold standard)
  • Thick smear - for rapid detection of malarial parasite
    • Quantification is done under an oil immersion lens
      • + - 1 to 10 parasites per 100-thick film field
      • ++ - 11 to 100 parasites per 100 thick film field
      • +++ - 10 to 10 per thick film field
      • ++++ - more than 10 per thick film field
    • At least 200 oil immersion fields should be examined before a film is declared negative.
    • It can be used for the detection of malarial parasites as low as 20 parasites / μL
 
  • Thin smear - for determination of plasmodium species

 
  • Stains used - Romanowsky stain (Leishman, Giemsa or JSB stain)

Quantitative buffy coat test
  • RBCs with parasites are less dense; thus, concentrate just below the buffy coat of WBC on top of the RBC column
  • Acridine orange is used to induce fluorescence on the parasite, giving a fluorescent greenish-yellow appearance on a red background
  • Microscopic examination of a smear made using the buffy coat is done.

Kawamoto fluorescence microscopy

  • Fluorescent dye like acridine orange or benzothiocarboxy purine is used to stain the parasite inside the RBC
  • Parasite DNA is stained fluorescent green, and cytosol RNA is stained red
  • The slide is examined under the fluorescent microscope
  • Used for mass screening in field laboratory

Rapid antigen detection test

  • Immunochromatography is done using monoclonal antibody directed against the parasite antigen

Parasite F test

  • Monoclonal antibody is used to detect histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2), which is produced by asexual stages of plasmodium falciparum
    • High sensitivity and specificity
    • Can detect low parasitemia (40 parasite / μL of blood)
    • Can detect only the asexual stage of plasmodium falciparum

Dual antigen test
  • Detects Parasite lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH) and Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein (PfHRP-2)
  • pLDH is produced by trophozoites and gametocytes of all plasmodium spp.
  • PfHRP-2 is produced only by the asexual stage of Plasmodium falciparum.

Molecular method

  • PCR: Used for species determination and detection of drug resistance.

Diarrhea is not a distinguishing feature of psoriatic arthritis; it is more commonly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)-related arthritis.

CASPAR Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA):

To classify a patient as having PsA, they must have inflammatory joint disease (affecting joints, spine, or entheses) plus ≥3 of the following 5 criteria:

  1. Evidence of Psoriasis (Any one of the following):
    • Current psoriasis
    • Personal history of psoriasis
    • Family history of psoriasis
  2. Psoriatic nail dystrophy (Option C ruled out)
  3. Negative Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
  4. Dactylitis (Current or past history) (Option B ruled out)
  5. Radiological evidence of juxta-articular new bone formation

Enthesitis (Option C): which is inflammation of tendons and ligaments, though not part of CASPAR criteria for PsA, is commonly found in PsA.

 

Note: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative polyarthritis with erosive arthritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the ideal maintenance fluid for pediatric patients?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the ideal maintenance fluid for pediatric patients?
questions.solution: The preferred fluid for fluid correction in pediatric patients is 5% dextrose and N saline (DNS) . Moreover, a maintenance dose of potassium, with 1ml of KCl per 100ml, is also added to the solution. DNS (Dextrose Normal Saline) is used in children as a maintenance fluid because: Prevents Hypoglycemia: Provides around 17 calories/ 100ml of 5%D as energy , crucial for children with higher metabolic rates. It also prevents ketone production and minimises protein degradation . Maintains Fluid and Electrolyte Balance: Sodium chloride in DNS preserves extracellular fluid volume and prevents dehydration. Isotonic Solution: Stabilizes intravascular volume without causing fluid shifts. Hypotonic fluids like N/2 and N/4 saline (Option A, C, D) can cause hyponatraemia and hemolysis. Hence Isotonic fluids with 5% dextrose are preferred as maintenance fluids in children @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Explanation: HLA-DQ6 and HLA-DQ11 are not associated with celiac disease. In contrast, HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 are the primary genetic markers found in almost all individuals with celiac disease. Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically predisposed individuals. It primarily affects the proximal small intestine, with the duodenum most commonly involved. In some cases, it extends to the jejunum, causing more severe symptoms. Pathophysiology: Genetics : HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 are associated with celiac disease. Immune Response : Gluten ingestion triggers inflammation in the small intestine Symptoms: Gastrointestinal : Diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, steatorrhea. Extra-intestinal : Fatigue, skin rashes (dermatitis herpetiformis), weight loss, anemia, joint pain, headaches, peripheral neuropathy. In Children : Delayed growth, irritability, poor weight gain, bone issues due to malabsorption. Diagnosis: 1. Serological Testing: Tissue Transglutaminase (tTG) Antibodies: Most sensitive and specific test. (Option A ruled out) Anti-Endomysial Antibodies (EMA) Anti-Gliadin Antibodies (AGA): Less specific. (Option B ruled out) 2. Histological Confirmation: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with small bowel biopsy is the gold standard. Histological Changes : Villous Atrophy : Flattened villi. {{caption_text}} Crypt Hyperplasia : Increased crypt cells. Intraepithelial Lymphocytosis : Elevated lymphocytes. 3. Histological Grading (Modified Marsh Classification): (Option C ruled out) Type Definition 0 Normal duodenal biopsy I Normal mucosal architecture with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes II Hyperplastic crypts, but near normal Villi IIIa Hyperplastic crypts with partial villous atrophy IIIb Hyperplastic crypts with subtotal villous atrophy IIIc Hyperplastic crypts with total villous atrophy Treatment: Gluten-Free Diet : Lifelong, strict adherence is the only treatment. Gluten-containing foods (BROW) : Barley, Rye, Oats, Wheat. Complications: Malnutrition : Due to impaired absorption. Osteoporosis : From poor calcium and vitamin D absorption. Intestinal Lymphoma and Small Bowel Cancer : Rare but serious. Increased Risk of Autoimmune Disorders : Such as Type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease. Feature Coeliac Sprue Whipple's Disease Tropical Sprue Description Autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten. Systemic infectious disease caused by Tropheryma whipplei. Malabsorption disorder seen in tropical regions. Cause often unknown, possibly infectious. Etiology Genetic predisposition (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). Environmental trigger: gluten (present in wheat, barley, rye) ingestion and an immune response to gliadin, a protein in gluten. Infection with Tropheryma whipplei, found in soil and sewage. Possibly due to bacterial, fungal or coronavirus infection. Clinical Features Affects mainly proximal small intestine. Intestinal Features: Chronic diarrhea or steatorrhea. Malabsorption: weight loss, vitamin deficiencies. Abdominal pain, bloating. Extraintestinal Features: Iron-deficiency anemia. Dermatitis herpetiformis (in some cases). Affects mainly distal small intestine. Intestinal Features: Chronic diarrhea. Malabsorption, weight loss. Abdominal pain and bloating. Extraintestinal Features: Arthralgia (joint pain). Fever. Lymphadenopathy. Neurological symptoms (cognitive impairment, seizures, ataxia in advanced stages, oculomasticatory myorhythmia). Uveitis Cardiac involvement (rare). Affects entire small intestinal Intestinal Features: Chronic diarrhea. Malabsorption, weight loss. Abdominal pain, bloating. Extraintestinal Features: Anemia (often megaloblastic). Histological Findings {{caption_text}} Loss or flattening of intestinal villi (villous atrophy). Hyperplastic crypts (crypt elongation). Increased infiltration of lymphocytes, especially CD8+ T cells. Increased plasma cells, lymphocytes, macrophages in lamina propria. {{caption_text}} Villous blunting and atrophy. Dense infiltration of lamina propria by macrophages containing PAS-positive granules. Foamy macrophages laden with Tropheryma whipplei in various tissues (e.g., lymph nodes, CNS, synovial fluid). {{caption_text}} Villous atrophy. Crypt hyperplasia. Increased inflammatory cells (similar to Celiac disease but without gliadin-specific immune response). Investigations Biopsy Serologic Tests: Most sensitive and most common antibody test: Anti-Tissue Transglutaminase Antibodies (Anti-tTG) - IgA and IgG Most specific antibody test: Anti-Endomysial Antibodies (EMA) - IgA. Anti-Deamidated Gliadin Peptide (DGP) Antibodies - IgA and IgG. Anti-Gliadin Antibodies (AGA) - IgA and IgG. Biopsy PCR for Tropheryma whipplei DNA. Immunohistochemistry for Tropheryma whipplei. Biopsy Response to Treatment: Antibiotic response helps confirm diagnosis. Management Lifelong gluten-free diet. Nutritional supplementation: iron, folate, calcium, vitamin D. Indications for steroids: Refractory disease for 6-12 months Celiac crisis Lymphoma Monitoring for complications Prolonged antibiotic therapy: Initially IV ceftriaxone or meropenem for 2 weeks. Followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a year. Tetracycline for 6 months. Folate supplementation. Some recommend a gluten-free diet. Complications Osteoporosis. Malignancy (e.g., small bowel lymphoma). Infertility. Neurological complications (rare). Failure to thrive. Untreated disease can be fatal due to multi-organ involvement. Relapses are common (especially CNS). Nutritional deficiencies can lead to osteoporosis, cachexia. Nutritional deficiencies (e.g., vitamin B12, folate). Persistent malabsorption. Possible relapse and chronic diarrhea. @Neet_pg_bot

Infection with Tropheryma whipplei, found in soil and sewage.
  • Possibly due to bacterial, fungal or coronavirus infection.

Clinical Features

Affects mainly proximal small intestine.

 

Intestinal Features:

  • Chronic diarrhea or steatorrhea.
  • Malabsorption: weight loss, vitamin deficiencies.
  • Abdominal pain, bloating.
 

Extraintestinal Features:

  • Iron-deficiency anemia.
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis (in some cases).

Affects mainly distal small intestine.

 

Intestinal Features:

  • Chronic diarrhea.
  • Malabsorption, weight loss.
  • Abdominal pain and bloating.
 

Extraintestinal Features:

  • Arthralgia (joint pain).
  • Fever.
  • Lymphadenopathy.
  • Neurological symptoms (cognitive impairment, seizures, ataxia in advanced stages, oculomasticatory myorhythmia).
  • Uveitis
  • Cardiac involvement (rare).

Affects entire small intestinal

 

Intestinal Features:

  • Chronic diarrhea.
  • Malabsorption, weight loss.
  • Abdominal pain, bloating.
 

Extraintestinal Features:

  • Anemia (often megaloblastic).

Histological Findings
 
  • Loss or flattening of intestinal villi (villous atrophy).
  • Hyperplastic crypts (crypt elongation).
  • Increased infiltration of lymphocytes, especially CD8+ T cells.
  • Increased plasma cells, lymphocytes, macrophages in lamina propria.
 
  • Villous blunting and atrophy.
  • Dense infiltration of lamina propria by macrophages containing PAS-positive granules.
  • Foamy macrophages laden with Tropheryma whipplei in various tissues (e.g., lymph nodes, CNS, synovial fluid).
 
  • Villous atrophy.
  • Crypt hyperplasia.
  • Increased inflammatory cells (similar to Celiac disease but without gliadin-specific immune response).

Investigations

Biopsy

Serologic Tests:

  • Most sensitive and most common antibody test: Anti-Tissue Transglutaminase Antibodies (Anti-tTG) - IgA and IgG
  • Most specific antibody test: Anti-Endomysial Antibodies (EMA) - IgA.
  • Anti-Deamidated Gliadin Peptide (DGP) Antibodies - IgA and IgG.
  • Anti-Gliadin Antibodies (AGA) - IgA and IgG.

Biopsy

PCR for Tropheryma whipplei DNA.

Immunohistochemistry for Tropheryma whipplei.

Biopsy

Response to Treatment: Antibiotic response helps confirm diagnosis.

Management
  • Lifelong gluten-free diet.
  • Nutritional supplementation: iron, folate, calcium, vitamin D.
  • Indications for steroids:
    • Refractory disease for 6-12 months
    • Celiac crisis
    • Lymphoma
  • Monitoring for complications

Prolonged antibiotic therapy:

  • Initially IV ceftriaxone or meropenem for 2 weeks.
  • Followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a year.
  • Tetracycline for 6 months.
  • Folate supplementation.
  • Some recommend a gluten-free diet.

Complications
  • Osteoporosis.
  • Malignancy (e.g., small bowel lymphoma).
  • Infertility.
  • Neurological complications (rare).
  • Failure to thrive.
  • Untreated disease can be fatal due to multi-organ involvement.
  • Relapses are common (especially CNS).
  • Nutritional deficiencies can lead to osteoporosis, cachexia.
  • Nutritional deficiencies (e.g., vitamin B12, folate).
  • Persistent malabsorption.
  • Possible relapse and chronic diarrhea.

questions.stem: A patient presented with a blood pressure of 220/120 mmHg in an altered sensorium. He also had an episode of vomiting and a history of weakness on the left side of his body. Which of the following is incorrect regarding hypertensive management in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with a blood pressure of 220/120 mmHg in an altered sensorium. He also had an episode of vomiting and a history of weakness on the left side of his body. Which of the following is incorrect regarding hypertensive management in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: In hemorrhagic stroke, reduce the BP to less than 160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to prevent rebleed

options.label: B
options.text: In hemorrhagic stroke, aggressive use of IV antihypertensive if SBP > 220

options.label: C
options.text: In the ER, multiple blood pressure readings should be taken before starting antihypertensive therapy

options.label: D
options.text: In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately

questions.answerText: In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately
questions.solution: In ischemic stroke, BP should not be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately. The correct management includes reducing the BP to <185/110 mmHg before administering thrombolytic therapy. Lowering BP too aggressively could compromise cerebral perfusion, potentially worsening the ischemia and increasing infarct size. Hemorrhagic Stroke: BP should be lowered to <160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to reduce the risk of rebleeding (Option A). If SBP > 220 mmHg, aggressive use of IV antihypertensives is recommended (Option B). Ischemic Stroke: BP should only be reduced to <185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis. If the BP is above this threshold and thrombolysis is considered, lowering it is necessary, but a reduction to <140/90 mmHg can worsen cerebral perfusion. Emergency Management: In a hypertensive emergency, multiple BP readings should be taken to ensure accurate assessment before starting antihypertensive therapy (Option C). This is important to avoid over- or under-treatment. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• In ischemic stroke, BP should not be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately.
  • The correct management includes reducing the BP to <185/110 mmHg before administering thrombolytic therapy.
  • Lowering BP too aggressively could compromise cerebral perfusion, potentially worsening the ischemia and increasing infarct size.

 

Hemorrhagic Stroke:

  • BP should be lowered to <160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to reduce the risk of rebleeding (Option A).
  • If SBP > 220 mmHg, aggressive use of IV antihypertensives is recommended (Option B).

 

Ischemic Stroke:

  • BP should only be reduced to <185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis.
  • If the BP is above this threshold and thrombolysis is considered, lowering it is necessary, but a reduction to <140/90 mmHg can worsen cerebral perfusion.

 

Emergency Management:

  • In a hypertensive emergency, multiple BP readings should be taken to ensure accurate assessment before starting antihypertensive therapy (Option C).
  • This is important to avoid over- or under-treatment.

questions.stem: What is the mutation seen in Sickle cell anemia?
questions.stemHtml: What is the mutation seen in Sickle cell anemia?
questions.solution: ="44044ded7116927772015bdce1fbc8">Val (6) Explanation: Sickle cell anemia is a genetic disorder caused by a missense mutation in the β-globin gene. This mutation replaces the normal glutamic acid (Glu) at position 6 of the β-globin chain with valine (Val). This Glu → Val substitution leads to the formation of hemoglobin S (HbS), which tends to polymerize when deoxygenated, causing the red blood cells to become sickle-shaped. These sickle-shaped cells are rigid and prone to breaking, leading to anemia and other complications. Pathophysiology of Sickle cell anemia {{caption_text}} HbS Polymerisation: A single-nucleotide polymorphism in the β-globin gene results in the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position in the β-globin chain. This mutation leads to the formation of mutated hemoglobin (HbS). After deoxygenation, HbS molecules polymerize to form bundles. These polymer bundles cause erythrocytes to adopt a sickle shape and also promote hemolysis of erythrocyte, releasing cell-free Hb into circulation. Vaso-occlusion: Sickled erythrocytes impair blood flow and aggregate with neutrophils, platelets, and endothelial cells, causing stasis. Leads to ischemia-reperfusion (I-R) injury. Endothelial Dysfunction: Oxygenated Hb (Fe²⁺) depletes endothelial nitric oxide (NO), forming nitrate (NO₃⁻) and methemoglobin (Fe³⁺). Free radicals are generated by NADPH oxidase, xanthine oxidase (XO), and uncoupled endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) contribute to endothelial damage and dysfunction. Methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) breaks down, releasing cell-free heme, which is a major erythrocyte damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP). Sterile Inflammation: Cell-free heme or ischemia-reperfusion injury triggers sterile inflammation by: Generating reactive oxygen species (ROS). Activating Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). Inducing neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). Releasing DAMPs, DNA, and other unidentified factors. This activates the inflammasome pathway, releasing IL-1β. Sterile inflammation enhances the adhesiveness of neutrophils, platelets, and endothelial cells. This creates a cycle that promotes further vaso-occlusion. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
="44044ded7116927772015bdce1fbc8">Val (6)

 

Explanation:

  • Sickle cell anemia is a genetic disorder caused by a missense mutation in the β-globin gene.
  • This mutation replaces the normal glutamic acid (Glu) at position 6 of the β-globin chain with valine (Val).

 

  • This Glu → Val substitution leads to the formation of hemoglobin S (HbS), which tends to polymerize when deoxygenated, causing the red blood cells to become sickle-shaped.
  • These sickle-shaped cells are rigid and prone to breaking, leading to anemia and other complications.

 

Pathophysiology of Sickle cell anemia

  • HbS Polymerisation:
    • A single-nucleotide polymorphism in the β-globin gene results in the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position in the β-globin chain.
    • This mutation leads to the formation of mutated hemoglobin (HbS).
    • After deoxygenation, HbS molecules polymerize to form bundles.
    • These polymer bundles cause erythrocytes to adopt a sickle shape and also promote hemolysis of erythrocyte, releasing cell-free Hb into circulation.
  • Vaso-occlusion:
    • Sickled erythrocytes impair blood flow and aggregate with neutrophils, platelets, and endothelial cells, causing stasis.
    • Leads to ischemia-reperfusion (I-R) injury.
  • Endothelial Dysfunction:
    • Oxygenated Hb (Fe²⁺) depletes endothelial nitric oxide (NO), forming nitrate (NO₃⁻) and methemoglobin (Fe³⁺).
    • Free radicals are generated by NADPH oxidase, xanthine oxidase (XO), and uncoupled endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) contribute to endothelial damage and dysfunction.
    • Methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) breaks down, releasing cell-free heme, which is a major erythrocyte damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP).
  • Sterile Inflammation:
    • Cell-free heme or ischemia-reperfusion injury triggers sterile inflammation by:
      • Generating reactive oxygen species (ROS).
      • Activating Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4).
      • Inducing neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).
      • Releasing DAMPs, DNA, and other unidentified factors.
    • This activates the inflammasome pathway, releasing IL-1β.
    • Sterile inflammation enhances the adhesiveness of neutrophils, platelets, and endothelial cells.
    • This creates a cycle that promotes further vaso-occlusion.

p>

Explanation:

  • After renal allograft transplantation, serum creatinine is one of the earliest and most sensitive indicators of graft dysfunction.
  • A rise in serum creatinine, even if small or unexplained, necessitates further investigation to rule out acute rejection.

 

Acute Renal Allograft Rejection

  • Acute renal allograft rejection occurs when the recipient's immune system identifies the transplanted kidney as foreign, leading to cellular or antibody-mediated immune responses that cause kidney inflammation and damage.

 

Clinical Presentation:

  • Typically occurs weeks to months post-transplant, but can occur later if immunosuppression is reduced.
  • Symptoms may include reduced urine output, graft tenderness, fever, and malaise, though not always present.
  • Any unexplained increase in creatinine should raise suspicion for acute rejection.

 

Types of Acute Rejection:

  • Cellular Rejection (T-cell Mediated): T-cells attack the graft, causing inflammation and tissue damage.
  • Antibody-Mediated Rejection (AMR): Antibodies attack the donor endothelial cells, leading to endothelial injury and microvascular thrombosis.

Confirmatory Investigation:

  • Renal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing acute rejection and determining the type of rejection.
  • Biopsy findings:
    • Cellular rejection: T-cell infiltration and inflammation.
    • AMR: Endothelial damage and microvascular inflammation.

Treatment:

  • Cellular rejection: Treated with increased immunosuppressive therapy (e.g., steroids, ATG).
  • AMR: Requires treatments like plasmapheresis, IVIG, or rituximab.

 

Type of Rejection

Hyperacute Rejection

Acute Rejection

Chronic Rejection

Acute Cellular Rejection

Acute Antibody-Mediated Rejection

Description
  • Occurs immediately after transplant.
  • Mediated by preformed antibodies against graft endothelial cells.
  • Occurs within days to weeks after transplant.
  • Mediated by CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells.

Antibodies bind to graft endothelial cells, leading to complement activation and inflammation.
  • Develops over months to years.
  • Mediated by T cells.

Timing

Minutes to hours after transplant.

Days to weeks after transplant.

Days to months after transplant.

Months to years after transplant.

Type of Hypersensitivity Reaction

Type 2 (Cytotoxic Hypersensitivity)

Type 4 (Cell-mediated Hypersensitivity)

Type 2 (Cytotoxic Hypersensitivity)

Type 4 (Cell-mediated Hypersensitivity)

Immunologic Mechanism
  • Pre-existing antibodies activate complement.
  • Causes endothelial injury and thrombosis.
  • CD8+ T cells destroy graft cells.
  • CD4+ T cells induce inflammation.
  • Antibodies against graft antigens activate complement.
  • Leads to graft inflammation.

T cell-mediated response causes graft fibrosis and dysfunction.

Treatment
  • No treatment.
  • Requires graft removal.

Immunosuppressive therapy (steroids, antithymocyte globulin).

Plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab, steroids.
  • No definitive treatment.
  • Supportive care and immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A known case of ulcerative colitis is not responding to an anti-TNF alpha agent. Which JAK inhibitor is preferred for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis?
questions.stemHtml: A known case of ulcerative colitis is not responding to an anti-TNF alpha agent. Which JAK inhibitor is preferred for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis?
questions.solution: l JAK inhibitor that works by inhibiting the JAK-STAT pathway, which regulates cytokine-mediated inflammation. It is approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis, particularly in patients who are refractory or intolerant to anti-TNF agents like infliximab or adalimumab. Tofacitinib is a JAK 1/3 inhibitor and blocks the production of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 and interferons. It is effective for inducing and maintaining remission in moderate to severe ulcerative colitis. Side effects include an increased risk of infections, venous thromboembolism, and lipid elevation, requiring careful patient selection and monitoring. Vedolizumab (Option A) is an anti-integrin monoclonal antibody targeting α4β7 integrin, used to treat moderate to severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Ozanimod (Option C) is an FDA-approved sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P1) receptor modulator for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis, reducing lymphocyte migration to the gut. Leflunomide (Option D) is a pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor primarily for rheumatoid arthritis treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
questions.solution: esis is actually preferred in refractory cases of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), especially when the condition does not improve after initial treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). The standard treatment for GBS involves the use of either IVIG or plasmapheresis, depending on the patient's condition and response to initial therapy. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is a n acute autoimmune disorder that affects the peripheral nervous system . It often leads to ascending paralysis , starting from the lower limbs and spreading upwards. GBS is considered a neurological emergency due to its potential to cause respiratory failure, autonomic dysfunction, and death without timely treatment. Incidence: GBS occurs in 1–2 cases per 100,000 individuals annually. Preceding Infections: In about two-thirds of AIDP cases , a preceding infection triggers an autoimmune response. Common infections include: Campylobacter jejuni Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) Zika virus Influenza These infections lead to molecular mimicry , where the immune system attacks nerve structures , particularly the myelin sheath , causing demyelination. Variants of Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Variant Description Autoantibodies Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP) Most common in Europe and North America, marked by segmental demyelination . IgG Anti-GM1 , IgG Anti-GQ1b Axonal Variants (AMAN/AMSAN) More prevalent in China and Japan, often linked with Campylobacter jejuni infection. IgG Anti-GM1 Miller Fisher Syndrome Characterized by a triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia , the best-recognized variant. Anti-GQ1b Autoantibodies in Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Diversity: GBS patients exhibit a range of autoantibodies targeting nerve cells and structures. Common Antibodies: The most common are anti-ganglioside antibodies , which appear in up to 50% of GBS cases . Prognostic Implications: The presence of anti-GM1 antibodies correlates with poorer clinical outcomes , especially in pure motor variants and Miller Fisher Syndrome . Clinical Features: Motor Symptoms Progressive ascending paralysis (distal to proximal) Areflexia Weakness in legs, causing rubbery legs and instability to stand Truncal paralysis, quadriplegia Difficulty handling secretions leading to aspiration pneumonia Diaphragmatic paralysis or bulbar palsy leading to respiratory failure within hours, Ventilatory support required in 30% of cases Sensory Symptoms Glove-and-stocking distribution paresthesias Loss of proprioception Pain in neck/shoulders similar to over-exercised muscles Autonomic Symptoms Orthostatic hypotension Wide fluctuations of blood pressure Arrhythmias Neurogenic shock Diagnostic Findings: Category Findings Lumbar Puncture Elevated CSF protein (100-1000 mg/dL) with normal WBC count (albuminocytologic dissociation) CSF Timing Normal findings (<48 hours), protein rise seen by 7 days Electrodiagnostic Testing Prolonged F-wave latencies, indicating demyelination (early in AIDP) Brighton Criteria for Diagnosis of GBS: Mnemonic: FAME F laccid Bilateral Weakness Areflexia (Option A) CytoAlbuminologic dissociation (Elevated CSF protein, normal WBC) (Option D) M onophasic Illness (Symptoms develop over 12 hours to 28 days) E lectrodiagnostic findings consistent with demyelination Treatment: IVIG (Intravenous Immunoglobulin) (Option C): First-line treatment. It modulates the immune response and helps reduce inflammation. Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange): ​​​​​​​ Equally effective as IVIG. questions.solutionHtml:
esis is actually preferred in refractory cases of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), especially when the condition does not improve after initial treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).
  • The standard treatment for GBS involves the use of either IVIG or plasmapheresis, depending on the patient's condition and response to initial therapy.

    •  

    Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)

    • Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disorder that affects the peripheral nervous system.
    • It often leads to ascending paralysis, starting from the lower limbs and spreading upwards.
    • GBS is considered a neurological emergency due to its potential to cause respiratory failure, autonomic dysfunction, and death without timely treatment.
    • Incidence: GBS occurs in 1–2 cases per 100,000 individuals annually.
    • Preceding Infections: In about two-thirds of AIDP cases, a preceding infection triggers an autoimmune response. Common infections include:
      • Campylobacter jejuni
      • Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
      • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
      • Zika virus
      • Influenza
    • These infections lead to molecular mimicry, where the immune system attacks nerve structures, particularly the myelin sheath, causing demyelination.

    Variants of Guillain-Barré Syndrome:

    Variant

    Description

    Autoantibodies

    Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP)

    Most common in Europe and North America, marked by segmental demyelination.

    IgG Anti-GM1, IgG Anti-GQ1b

    Axonal Variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

    More prevalent in China and Japan, often linked with Campylobacter jejuni infection.

    IgG Anti-GM1

    Miller Fisher Syndrome

    Characterized by a triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, the best-recognized variant.

    Anti-GQ1b

     

    Autoantibodies in Guillain-Barré Syndrome:

    • Diversity: GBS patients exhibit a range of autoantibodies targeting nerve cells and structures.
    • Common Antibodies: The most common are anti-ganglioside antibodies, which appear in up to 50% of GBS cases.
    • Prognostic Implications: The presence of anti-GM1 antibodies correlates with poorer clinical outcomes, especially in pure motor variants and Miller Fisher Syndrome.

    Clinical Features:

    Motor Symptoms
    • Progressive ascending paralysis (distal to proximal)
    • Areflexia
    • Weakness in legs, causing rubbery legs and instability to stand
    • Truncal paralysis, quadriplegia
    • Difficulty handling secretions leading to aspiration pneumonia
    • Diaphragmatic paralysis or bulbar palsy leading to respiratory failure within hours, Ventilatory support required in 30% of cases

    Sensory Symptoms
    • Glove-and-stocking distribution paresthesias
    • Loss of proprioception
    • Pain in neck/shoulders similar to over-exercised muscles

    Autonomic Symptoms
    • Orthostatic hypotension
    • Wide fluctuations of blood pressure
    • Arrhythmias
    • Neurogenic shock

     

    Diagnostic Findings:

    Category

    Findings

    Lumbar Puncture

    Elevated CSF protein (100-1000 mg/dL) with normal WBC count (albuminocytologic dissociation)

    CSF Timing

    Normal findings (<48 hours), protein rise seen by 7 days

    Electrodiagnostic Testing

    Prolonged F-wave latencies, indicating demyelination (early in AIDP)

     

    Brighton Criteria for Diagnosis of GBS:

    Mnemonic: FAME

    Flaccid Bilateral Weakness

    Areflexia (Option A)

    CytoAlbuminologic dissociation (Elevated CSF protein, normal WBC) (Option D)

    Monophasic Illness (Symptoms develop over 12 hours to 28 days)

    Electrodiagnostic findings consistent with demyelination

     

    Treatment:

    • IVIG (Intravenous Immunoglobulin) (Option C):
      • First-line treatment.
      • It modulates the immune response and helps reduce inflammation.
    • Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange):
      • ​​​​​​​Equally effective as IVIG.
      • It removes harmful antibodies from the blood; preferred in refractory cases.
    • Glucocorticoids:
      • Not useful in GBS treatment, as they do not improve outcomes.

Ankylosing Spondylitis

 

Clinical Features

General Features

Spine and Joint involvement

Extra-articular manifestations

Causes: Glomerulonephritis (Post-streptococcal, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, membranoproliferative GN) Small Vessel Vasculitis (ANCA-associated vasculitis, Goodpasture’s syndrome) Hereditary Conditions (Alport syndrome, Thin basement membrane disease) Features Color: Cola-colored or smoky brown urine Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes, Mickey Mouse cells) Proteinuria: Often present, especially if associated with nephritic syndrome Presence of RBC casts (diagnostic of glomerular origin) Clots absent (distinguishes from non-glomerular hematuria) Serum Markers : Often associated with increased serum creatinine. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
n:

Glomerular hematuria presents with brown-colored urine due to RBC breakdown, absence of dysuria as it is not due to lower urinary tract infection, and edema may occur in nephritic syndrome, but is not rare; however, crystals are not a feature of glomerular hematuria.

 

Glomerular Hematuria

Glomerular hematuria occurs due to damage to the glomerular filtration barrier, leading to the leakage of red blood cells (RBCs) into the urine.

 

Causes:

  • Glomerulonephritis (Post-streptococcal, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, membranoproliferative GN)
  • Small Vessel Vasculitis (ANCA-associated vasculitis, Goodpasture’s syndrome)
  • Hereditary Conditions (Alport syndrome, Thin basement membrane disease)

 

Features

  • Color: Cola-colored or smoky brown urine
  • Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes, Mickey Mouse cells)
  • Proteinuria: Often present, especially if associated with nephritic syndrome
  • Presence of RBC casts (diagnostic of glomerular origin)
  • Clots absent (distinguishes from non-glomerular hematuria)

 

Serum Markers: Often associated with increased serum creatinine.

  • Behçet’s Disease is a chronic, multisystemic vasculitis characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, and systemic involvement.
  • It is an immune-mediated disorder that primarily affects small and medium-sized blood vessels.

 

Behcet’s Disease- Pathogenesis and Clinical Features

Category

Features

Clinical Significance

Pathogenesis
  • T-cell mediated immunity
  • Th1 cell activation
  • Elevated cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α)
  • Neutrophilic vasculitis
  • No specific autoantibodies
  • Auto-inflammatory rather than autoimmune
  • Affects vessels of all sizes
  • Treatment targets inflammation

Mucocutaneous
  • Oral ulcers (97-99%)
  • Genital ulcers (>80%)
  • Erythema nodosum
  • Pathergy reaction
  • Often initial presentation
  • Oral ulcers heal without scarring
  • Genital ulcers leave scars

Major Organ Involvement
  • B/L uveitis (>50%) (Option C)
  • Vascular (25%)
  • Neurologic (5-10%)
  • Arthritis (non-erosive)
  • More severe in males
  • Ocular disease can cause blindness
  • Vascular involvement can be fatal
  • Presents similar to IBD (Crohn's disease > Ulcerative colitis) (Option B)

Behcet’s Disease- Diagnosis and Management

Diagnosis

Diagnostic Criteria (ITR-ICBD)

Two Points Each:

  • Genital aphthosis
  • Ocular lesions
 

One Point Each:

  • Oral aphthosis
  • Skin lesions
  • Vascular manifestations
  • Positive pathergy (Option D)

≥3 points needed for diagnosis

Laboratory Findings
  • Non-specific inflammation markers
  • No specific autoantibodies
  • ESR, CRP elevation
  • Leukocytosis

Helps rule out other conditions

Required Investigations
  • Ophthalmologic examination
  • Pathergy test
  • Skin biopsy if needed
  • Imaging, based on symptoms

Confirms involvement and monitors complications

Treatment

Mucocutaneous Treatment
  • Colchicine 1-2mg/day
  • Topical steroids
  • Topical sucralfate

Refractory: Systemic steroids, azathioprine

Ocular Treatment
  • Anterior: Topical steroids
  • Posterior: Steroids + azathioprine

Refractory: TNF inhibitors

Major Organ Involvement
  • Vascular: High-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide
  • Neurologic: High-dose steroids + immunosuppression

Requires aggressive therapy and monitoring

Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia (ARVD) is an inherited cardiac disorder characterized by the progressive replacement of the right ventricular myocardium with fibrofatty tissue, leading to arrhythmias, particularly ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death. It primarily affects the right ventricle but can involve the left ventricle as well. Etiology Mutations in genes encoding desmosomal proteins (e.g., PKP2, DSP, DSG2, JUP). Clinical Features Palpitations Syncope Exercise-induced arrhythmias Sudden cardiac death, Particularly in young, athletic individuals. Echocardiography: May show right ventricular dilation and dysfunction. Cardiac MRI: Shows fibrofatty infiltration of the right ventricle. Family history: Key in diagnosing genetic basis. Diagnostic Criteria Based on the Task Force Criteria, which include: ECG abnormalities, arrhythmias, imaging findings, and histological evidence. Pathological criteria: Fibrofatty infiltration of the right ventricle. Management Antiarrhythmic drugs Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD): For preventing sudden cardiac death in high-risk patients. Heart transplantation: In severe cases with progressive heart failure. Uhl's disease (Option A): Also affects the right ventricle but lacks the hallmark epsilon waves and T-wave inversions. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (Option C): More commonly presents with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and deep Q waves, not epsilon waves. Brugada’s Syndrome (Option D): Characterized by ST-segment elevation in V1–V3, not epsilon waves. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Dysplasia

 

Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms of palpitations, syncope following exercise, and a suggestive ECG pattern are characteristic of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia (ARVD), a condition that often leads to arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, particularly in young, athletic individuals.
  • Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia (ARVD) is an inherited cardiac disorder characterized by the progressive replacement of the right ventricular myocardium with fibrofatty tissue, leading to arrhythmias, particularly ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death.
  • It primarily affects the right ventricle but can involve the left ventricle as well.

 

Etiology

  • Mutations in genes encoding desmosomal proteins (e.g., PKP2, DSP, DSG2, JUP).

 

Clinical Features

  • Palpitations
  • Syncope
  • Exercise-induced arrhythmias
  • Sudden cardiac death, Particularly in young, athletic individuals.

 

Diagnostic Findings

Electrocardiogram (ECG):

  • Ventricular arrhythmias, especially ventricular tachycardia.
  • Epsilon waves on ECG (specific to ARVD).

 

Echocardiography: May show right ventricular dilation and dysfunction.

Cardiac MRI: Shows fibrofatty infiltration of the right ventricle.

Family history: Key in diagnosing genetic basis.

 

Diagnostic Criteria

Based on the Task Force Criteria, which include:

 

  • ECG abnormalities, arrhythmias, imaging findings, and histological evidence.
  • Pathological criteria: Fibrofatty infiltration of the right ventricle.

 

Management

  • Antiarrhythmic drugs
  • Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD): For preventing sudden cardiac death in high-risk patients.
  • Heart transplantation: In severe cases with progressive heart failure.

 

Uhl's disease (Option A): Also affects the right ventricle but lacks the hallmark epsilon waves and T-wave inversions.

 

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (Option C): More commonly presents with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and deep Q waves, not epsilon waves.

 

Brugada’s Syndrome (Option D): Characterized by ST-segment elevation in V1–V3, not epsilon waves.

questions.stem: All are hereditary causes of thrombosis except:
questions.stemHtml: All are hereditary causes of thrombosis except:
questions.solution: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare acquired condition marked by clonal expansion of hematopoietic stem cells lacking GPI anchor proteins and is not a hereditary cause of thrombosis. PNH blood cells are deficient in three GPI-linked proteins that regulate complement activity: CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis) C8-binding protein. Pathogenesis: It results from acquired mutations in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of certain membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. Clinical features: It causes intravascular haemolysis and anaemia Haemoglobinuria (red-brown colour) (most noticeable in early morning urine) Hypoplastic bone marrow failure, aplastic anaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome Management Transfusion Folate supplements Prophylaxis or treatment of thrombosis Anti-complement C5 monoclonal antibody. Protein S deficiency (Option B) is a genetic disorder that increases the risk of abnormal blood clotting (thrombosis). Protein C and its co-factor protein S are vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulants involved in switching off coagulation factor activation (factors Va and VIIIa) and thrombin generation. Deficiency can lead to deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), and other thrombotic events. Antithrombin deficiency (Option C) is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder that heightens the risk of abnormal blood clotting (thrombosis). Antithrombin (AT) is a serine protease inhibitor (SERPIN) that inactivates activated coagulation factors IIa, IXa, Xa, and XIa. A deficiency in AT can result in deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), and other thrombotic events. Heparins and fondaparinux enhance AT activity to exert their therapeutic effects. Homocystinuria (Option D) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CBS gene, leading to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency that results in the accumulation of homocysteine and methionine in the blood. Symptoms include lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), intellectual disability, seizures, skeletal abnormalities similar to Marfan's syndrome, osteoporosis, thrombosis, and hyperpigmentation. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

Factor V Leiden mutation is the most common cause of inherited coagulopathy among the given options.

 

Hypercoagulability

  • It refers to an increased tendency of the blood to clot, usually due to changes in coagulation factors.
  • Types:
    • Primary disorders (genetic)
    • Secondary disorders (acquired)
  • Among inherited causes, point mutations in the factor V and prothrombin genes are the most common.

 

Primary disorders (Genetic)

Secondary disorders (Acquired)

Common

  • Factor V mutation
    • A single-nucleotide mutation (autosomal dominant inheritance) in the factor V gene makes factor V resistant to cleavage and inactivation by protein C.
  • Prothrombin mutation
    • A single nucleotide change (G20210A) in the 3′-untranslated region of the prothrombin gene is linked to hypercoagulability.
 

Rare

  • Antithrombin III deficiency (Option B)
  • Protein C deficiency (Option C)
  • Protein S deficiency (Option D)
 

Very rare

  • Fibrinolysis defects
  • Homozygous homocystinuria (deficiency of cystathionine β-synthetase)

Strong Risk Factors for Thrombosis

  • Prolonged bed rest or immobilization
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Atrial fibrillation
  • Tissue injury (surgery, fracture, burn)
  • Cancer
  • Prosthetic cardiac valves
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
  • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
 

Other Risk Factors for Thrombosis

  • Cardiomyopathy
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy and postpartum)
  • Oral contraceptive use
  • Sickle cell anemia
  • Smoking

questions.solution: p> The described scenario, featuring a hand lesion and histopathological findings of encapsulated tissue with areas of dense cellularity and loose myxoid regions, suggests a diagnosis of Schwannoma . Schwannomas are benign tumours exhibiting Schwann cell differentiation and originate directly from peripheral nerves. (Option A) It is associated with NF2 mutations on chromosome 22 , producing merlin . (Option C) Most common location: Cerebellopontine angle Microscopically, they are comprised of: Antoni A area: Dense eosinophilic areas containing spindle cells are arranged into intersecting fascicles, leading to nuclei palisading. The resulting structures with central “nuclear-free zones” are called Verocay bodies . (Option B) Antoni B area: Loose, hypocellular areas where a myxoid extracellular matrix spreads apart the spindle cells. It typically shows immunoreactivity to S-100 . Clinical features: Cause symptoms by local compression of the involved nerve or adjacent structures (e.g., brainstem or spinal cord). Mostly occurs at the cerebellopontine angle (attached to the vestibular branch of the 8th nerve). Presents with tinnitus and hearing loss Sensory nerves are involved (trigeminal nerve and dorsal roots). They can arise in association with large nerve trunks or as soft tissue lesions (extradural) Management: Surgical removal is curative. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

The described scenario, featuring a hand lesion and histopathological findings of encapsulated tissue with areas of dense cellularity and loose myxoid regions, suggests a diagnosis of Schwannoma.

 

  • Schwannomas are benign tumours exhibiting Schwann cell differentiation and originate directly from peripheral nerves. (Option A)
  • It is associated with NF2 mutations on chromosome 22, producing merlin. (Option C)
  • Most common location: Cerebellopontine angle
  • Microscopically, they are comprised of:
    • Antoni A area: Dense eosinophilic areas containing spindle cells are arranged into intersecting fascicles, leading to nuclei palisading. The resulting structures with central “nuclear-free zones” are called Verocay bodies. (Option B)
    • Antoni B area: Loose, hypocellular areas where a myxoid extracellular matrix spreads apart the spindle cells.

  • It typically shows immunoreactivity to S-100.
  • Clinical features:
    • Cause symptoms by local compression of the involved nerve or adjacent structures (e.g., brainstem or spinal cord).
    • Mostly occurs at the cerebellopontine angle (attached to the vestibular branch of the 8th nerve).
    • Presents with tinnitus and hearing loss
    • Sensory nerves are involved (trigeminal nerve and dorsal roots).
    • They can arise in association with large nerve trunks or as soft tissue lesions (extradural)

Management: Surgical removal is curative.

questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation, along with histopathological and flow cytometry findings, confirms a diagnosis of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) with a B-cell phenotype based on the following results:
  • Histopathological examination reveals lymphoblasts with condensed nuclear chromatin, small nucleoli, and scant agranular cytoplasm.


  • Flow cytometry analysis:
    • Image B: The lymphoblasts (indicated by red dots) expressing terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and the B-cell marker CD22.
    • Image C: The cells test positive for two other markers, CD10 and CD19, commonly found on pre-B lymphoblasts.

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)

ALL is an acute-onset blood and bone marrow malignancy of B and T lymphoblasts characterised by the uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal and immature lymphocytes

Clinical features

  • Age: 2-8 years (Fast disease progression), adults: > 50 years.
  • Weight loss, Night sweats
  • Anemia: Easy fatigability and pallor
  • Bleeding: Epistaxis, easy bruising.
  • Leucocytopenia: Recurrent infections
  • Bone Marrow proliferation: Bone pain, sternal tenderness
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, Lymphadenopathy
  • CNS leukemia: Raised ICP, vomiting, and 6th nerve palsy
  • T cell tumors: Mediastinal and testicular mass.

Diagnosis

CBC is the first investigation performed while suspecting ALL:

  • Hemoglobin (Hb): Decreased, indicating normocytic normochromic anemia.
  • Hyperleukocytosis: TLC >100,000/µL can lead to leukostasis (more common in AML than ALL) with >20% Blasts.
  • Elderly Presentation: TLC often remains low throughout ALL.
  • Thrombocytopenia may be present.
 

Peripheral smear:

The smear shows a high percentage of lymphoblasts, which are larger than normal lymphocytes and have a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio. They often have a scant amount of cytoplasm and may exhibit nucleoli.

 

Bone Marrow aspiration shows blasts >20%.

  • It is also used to classify morphological types into L1, L2, and L3 in the FAB classification system.
 

FISH- Fluorescent in situ hybridization shows translocation of genes/chromosomes.

  • t(9:22) - ALL associated with the Philadelphia chromosome.
  • t(8:14) - Associated with Burkitt's leukemia
  • t(4:11)
  • t(1:19)
 

Flow cytometry:

  • CD10, also known as common acute lymphoblastic leukaemia antigen (CALLA), is a cell surface marker commonly used in the classification and diagnosis of leukaemias and lymphomas, particularly acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL).
  • B cell type - CD19+, CD79a+. (Option C)
  • T cell type - CD3+ (Option D ruled out)

 

Acute myeloid leukaemia (Option A) is a malignancy of hematopoietic progenitors caused by oncogenic mutations that prevent differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts. These blasts have delicate chromatin, two to four nucleoli, and more cytoplasm than lymphoblasts, often containing peroxidase-positive azurophilic granules. Auer rods, needle-like azurophilic granules, are also commonly present.

CLL (Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia) (Option B) is characterised by lymph node infiltration with small lymphocytes featuring condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm, along with larger activated lymphocytes forming proliferation centres, which are pathognomonic for CLL/SLL. The blood shows small lymphocytes and smudge cells, while the bone marrow, spleen, and liver are typically involved to varying degrees.
