questions.stem: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition induced by which pair of transcription factors?
questions.stemHtml: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition induced by which pair of transcription factors?
questions.solution: rong> Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is induced by the transcription factors SNAIL and TWIST. It is a process where epithelial cells lose their polarity and cell-cell adhesion, gaining migratory and invasive properties to transform into mesenchymal stem cells, multipotent stromal cells. t is hypothesized that E-cadherin (transmembrane glycoproteins that mediate the homotypic adhesion of epithelial cells) expression is transiently silenced through this process. It is controlled by the transcription factors SNAIL and TWIST. There is downregulation of epithelial markers (e.g., E-cadherin) and also upregulation of mesenchymal markers (e.g., vimentin and smooth muscle actin). TF IIA & TF IIB (Option A) are essential general transcription factors that are key to the initiation of transcription by RNA polymerase II. TFIIA contributes to transcriptional regulation by modulating the initiation process and ensuring correct gene expression. TFIIB is responsible for forming the transcription initiation complex and facilitating the transition from initiation to elongation. Cathepsin & MMP 8 (Matrix Metalloproteinase-8) (Option B) are enzymes that degrade proteins in the extracellular matrix, playing key roles in tissue remodelling and inflammation. Cathepsins aid in wound healing and immune responses but can contribute to cancer metastasis and inflammation. Elevated MMP-8 is linked to diseases like periodontal disease, arthritis, and cancer, where it contributes to tissue damage and remodelling. STAT-5 & HIF-1 alpha (Option D) are transcription factors. STAT-5, activated by cytokine receptors, regulates cell survival, differentiation, and immune responses and is key in hematopoiesis and cancers like leukaemia. HIF-1 alpha responds to low oxygen levels, activating genes for angiogenesis, metabolism, and erythropoiesis, and plays a critical role in tumour growth in hypoxic environments. @Neet_pg_bot

TFIIA contributes to transcriptional regulation by modulating the initiation process and ensuring correct gene expression. questions.solutionHtml:
hin the first 60 days of life, not 90 days. Delaying it beyond 60 days significantly decreases its success rate and heightens the likelihood of needing a liver transplant.

 

Neonatal cholestasis

Neonatal cholestasis is an abnormal accumulation of conjugated bilirubin (CB) due to impaired formation or flow of bile. Conjugated bilirubin exceeding 1 mg/dL is strongly suggestive of it.

 

Causes of neonatal cholestasis:

 

Category

Condition

Surgical (Extrahepatic)
  • Biliary atresia (EHBA) (Most common) (Option C)
  • Choledochal cyst
  • Cholelithiasis
  • Inspissated bile secretion
  • Spontaneous perforation of the bile duct
  • Nonsyndromic paucity of bile ducts
  • Congenital hepatic fibrosis/Caroli disease
  • Neonatal sclerosing cholangitis

Medical (Hepatocellular)
  • Idiopathic neonatal hepatitis
  • Prematurity
  • Viral infections (CMV, TORCH, HIV, etc.)
  • Bacterial infections (sepsis, UTI, syphilis, tuberculosis)
  • Hypothyroidism/ Hyperthyroidism/ Hypopituitarism
  • Galactosemia
  • Alagille syndrome
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • α1-antitrypsin deficiency
  • Indian childhood cirrhosis
  • Tyrosinemia
  • Fructosemia
  • Neonatal hemochromatosis
  • Gaucher disease
  • Wolman disease

 

Extra-Hepatic Biliary Atresia (EHBA)

Definition:

  • Biliary atresia not associated with cyst formation.
  • Also known as Non-Cystic Obliterative Cholangiopathy.
  • Characterized by complete obliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts and intrahepatic ducts at the hilum.

Symptoms:

  • Typically appear by 2 to 6 weeks of age
    • Jaundice (yellowish coloration of skin and sclera)
    • Abnormally pale stools
    • Dark urine

Association with other Anomalies:

  • The most common is polysplenia or asplenia
  • Other associated malformations include absent inferior vena cava, cardiac anomalies, situs inversus, intestinal malrotation, duodenal atresia, anomaly of the portal vein, renal anomalies, and choledochal cyst.

Investigations:

  1. Liver Function Tests:
    • Increased conjugated bilirubin.
    • Markers of cholestasis:
      • 5' nucleotidase
      • Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
      • GGT (Gamma-glutamyl transferase):
        • Normal: Up to 40 U/L
        • 4x elevation: Intrahepatic causes
        • 10x elevation: Extrahepatic causes
        • Exception: Low in PFIC type I and II
  2. Ultrasound:
    • High-frequency USG (HUS) for neonatal cholestasis.
    • Used as initial investigation
    • Fasting USG is the gold standard when biliary atresia is suspected.
    • Characteristic findings:
      • Triangular cord sign (hyperechoic areas indicating fibrous/atretic bile duct)
      • Non-visualized gallbladder/microgallbladder/gallbladder ghost
  3. Radionucleotide Study:
    • HIDA Scan (Option B) is investigation of choice (Hepatobiliary scan with Tc labelled imino-di-acetic acid):
      • Used as a screening test.
      • Decreased tracer excretion due to obstruction
    • Phenobarbitone loading/priming (5 days) to improve tracer uptake
    • Used as a screening test, not specific
  4. Best Investigation:
    • Liver biopsy (Option D): Confirms diagnosis.

Surgical Management:

  1. Algorithm:
    • Exploratory laparotomy
    • Per Operative cholangiogram
    • Temporary procedure: Kasai procedure/hepaticojejunostomy
    • Definitive management: Liver transplantation
  2. Kasai Procedure:
    • Temporary procedure
    • Creates communication between liver and jejunum for bile drainage
    • Also known as hepaticojejunostomy
    • Should be performed within 8 weeks after birth

questions.solutionHtml:
on:

Croup, also known as laryngotracheobronchitis, is an upper respiratory tract infection that causes barking cough, stridor, and hoarseness due to inflammation of the larynx and trachea. It is most commonly caused by the parainfluenza virus, followed by the influenza virus. Among the given options, the influenza virus is the most appropriate choice.


 

Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup): Viral infection of the glottic and subglottic regions

 

Causative Agent
  • Parainfluenza viruses (types 1,2 and 3) cause about 75% cases.
  • Other Viruses:
    • Influenza A and B,
    • Adenovirus,
    • Respiratory syncytial virus,
    • Measles.

Age Group
  • Most common in children aged 3 months to 5 years.
  • Peak incidence occurs in the 2nd year of life.

Initial Symptoms

These symptoms last 1-3 days before development of upper airway obstruction signs and symptoms.

  • Upper respiratory tract infection
  • Rhinorrhea
  • Pharyngitis
  • Mild cough
  • Low-grade fever

Progressive Symptoms

  • Barking cough
  • Hoarseness
  • Inspiratory stridor
  • Fever may reach 39- 40°C (102.2-104°F) or be absent
  • The child prefers to sit up in bed or be held upright
  • Symptoms worsen at night, recur over days and resolve within a week

Physical Examination Findings
  • Hoarse voice
  • Coryza
  • Inflamed pharynx
  • Slightly increased respiratory rate
  • Hypoxia and low oxygen saturation seen only in complete airway obstruction

Diagnosis

  • Clinical diagnosis
  • X-ray PA view of neck: Steeple sign, which is characteristic of subglottic narrowing

 

Treatment

  • Mainstay of Treatment: Focus on airway management and hypoxia treatment (O2).
  • Nebulized Racemic Epinephrine
  • Corticosteroids (dexamethasone):
    • Decrease edema in laryngeal mucosa
    • Oral steroids beneficial in mild croup
  • Antibiotics are not indicated.

 

Hemophilus influenza (Option A) is associated with epiglottitis, not croup.

 

Streptococcus pneumonia (Option B) is associated with pneumonia, otitis media, or meningitis, but not croup.

 

Diphtheria (Option D) is associated with diphtheria, which presents with a pseudomembrane in the throat and can lead to airway obstruction, but it is distinct from croup.

questions.answerText: Exclusive breastfeeding with total bilirubin >10mg/dl after 3-4 weeks of birth
questions.solution: n >10mg/dl after 3-4 weeks of birth Explanation: Approximately 2-4% of term neonates who are exclusively breastfed may have total serum bilirubin (TSB) levels exceeding 10 mg/dL beyond the third or fourth week of life. They are diagnosed to have breast milk jaundice. Breast milk jaundice (BMJ) should be considered in these infants if the jaundice is of the unconjugated type (not causing staining of nappies) and other causes of prolonged hyperbilirubinemia, such as insufficient feeding, ongoing hemolysis, blood extravasation, G6PD deficiency, and hypothyroidism, have been excluded. Breast milk contains elevated levels of beta-glucuronidase, which deconjugates bilirubin that has been conjugated by the liver and excreted into the intestine (Option D ruled out) . Most of these infants do not develop dangerously high TSB levels and typically do not require treatment (Option B ruled out) . Mothers can safely continue breastfeeding their infants, as there is no need to discontinue breastfeeding (Option A ruled out) for either the diagnosis or treatment of BMJ. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:
Approximately 2-4% of term neonates who are exclusively breastfed may have total serum bilirubin (TSB) levels exceeding 10 mg/dL beyond the third or fourth week of life. They are diagnosed to have breast milk jaundice.

  • Breast milk jaundice (BMJ) should be considered in these infants if the jaundice is of the unconjugated type (not causing staining of nappies) and other causes of prolonged hyperbilirubinemia, such as insufficient feeding, ongoing hemolysis, blood extravasation, G6PD deficiency, and hypothyroidism, have been excluded.
  • Breast milk contains elevated levels of beta-glucuronidase, which deconjugates bilirubin that has been conjugated by the liver and excreted into the intestine (Option D ruled out).
  • Most of these infants do not develop dangerously high TSB levels and typically do not require treatment (Option B ruled out).
  • Mothers can safely continue breastfeeding their infants, as there is no need to discontinue breastfeeding (Option A ruled out) for either the diagnosis or treatment of BMJ.

questions.solution: 927771829871a1737f">atresia is not a characteristic feature of cystic fibrosis. While cystic fibrosis can cause liver damage and biliary cirrhosis due to obstructed bile ducts, biliary atresia is a separate congenital condition where there is a complete absence or abnormality of the bile ducts, leading to severe liver damage and jaundice. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7q31.2 ( m/c mutation is ΔF508), leading to a defective CFTR protein. Pathophysiology of Cystic Fibrosis: CFTR Protein Dysfunction Defective chloride transport across epithelial cells Increased sodium absorption Decreased water movement leading to dehydrated mucous surfaces Respiratory System Thick, viscous mucus leads to airway obstruction and bacterial colonization Chronic infection and inflammation Bronchiectasis, atelectasis, and respiratory failure Gastrointestinal System Thick secretions block pancreatic ducts leading to enzyme insufficiency Malabsorption of fats and proteins Meconium ileus in neonates Distal Intestinal Obstruction Syndrome (DIOS) Hepatobiliary System Bile duct obstruction leading to biliary cirrhosis Sweat Glands Impaired chloride reabsorption leading to salty sweat Reproductive System Congenital absence of the vas deferens in males leading to azoospermia and infertility. Defective CFTR in the cervix leads to the production of thick, dehydrated cervical mucus that blocks the cervical os, impairing sperm entry and reducing fertility. Clinical Features of Cystic Fibrosis System Clinical Features Respiratory Chronic productive cough Recurrent respiratory infections Nasal polyps (Option A ruled out) Bronchiectasis Gastrointestinal Greasy stools (steatorrhea) Failure to thrive Rectal prolapse Malabsorption Meconium ileus in newborns (Option C ruled out) Genitourinary Infertility in males (due to congenital absence of vas deferens), delayed puberty Others Digital clubbing, Bleeding diathesis (Option D ruled out) , salt loss syndromes (hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis) @Neet_pg_bot

While cystic fibrosis can cause liver damage and biliary cirrhosis due to obstructed bile ducts, biliary atresia is a separate congenital condition where there is a complete absence or abnormality of the bile ducts, leading to severe liver damage and jaundice.
  • Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7q31.2 (m/c mutation is ΔF508), leading to a defective CFTR protein.

    •  

    Pathophysiology of Cystic Fibrosis:

     

    CFTR Protein Dysfunction
    • Defective chloride transport across epithelial cells
    • Increased sodium absorption
    • Decreased water movement leading to dehydrated mucous surfaces

    Respiratory System
    • Thick, viscous mucus leads to airway obstruction and bacterial colonization
    • Chronic infection and inflammation
    • Bronchiectasis, atelectasis, and respiratory failure

    Gastrointestinal System
    • Thick secretions block pancreatic ducts leading to enzyme insufficiency
    • Malabsorption of fats and proteins
    • Meconium ileus in neonates
    • Distal Intestinal Obstruction Syndrome (DIOS)

    Hepatobiliary System
    • Bile duct obstruction leading to biliary cirrhosis

    Sweat Glands
    • Impaired chloride reabsorption leading to salty sweat

    Reproductive System
    • Congenital absence of the vas deferens in males leading to azoospermia and infertility.
    • Defective CFTR in the cervix leads to the production of thick, dehydrated cervical mucus that blocks the cervical os, impairing sperm entry and reducing fertility.

    Clinical Features of Cystic Fibrosis

     

    System

    Clinical Features

    Respiratory
    • Chronic productive cough
    • Recurrent respiratory infections
    • Nasal polyps (Option A ruled out)
    • Bronchiectasis

    Gastrointestinal
    • Greasy stools (steatorrhea)
    • Failure to thrive
    • Rectal prolapse
    • Malabsorption
    • Meconium ileus in newborns (Option C ruled out)

    Genitourinary

    Infertility in males (due to congenital absence of vas deferens),

    delayed puberty

    Others

    Digital clubbing, Bleeding diathesis (Option D ruled out), salt loss syndromes (hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis)

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant presents with a history of epistaxis and recurrent rectal bleeding. The parents also reported a history of bleeding from the umbilicus since birth. Laboratory investigations revealed normal prothrombin time (PT), normal thrombin time, normal activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), normal platelet count, and normal function. Urea clot solubility test was positive. What is the most likely deficient factor in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 2-week-old infant presents with a history of epistaxis and recurrent rectal bleeding. The parents also reported a history of bleeding from the umbilicus since birth. Laboratory investigations revealed normal prothrombin time (PT), normal thrombin time, normal activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), normal platelet count, and normal function. Urea clot solubility test was positive. What is the most likely deficient factor in this patient?
questions.solution: feature is characteristic of Factor XIII (FXIII) deficiency / Laki lorand factor deficiency. It is a rare bleeding disorder that presents with symptoms spanning from delayed umbilical cord separation to intracranial hemorrhage. FXIII plays a pivotal role in stabilizing clots and facilitating the cross-linking of the fibrin polymer, thereby ensuring effective hemostasis The acquired FXIII deficiency typically arises from factors such as hyperconsumption, hemodilution, and decreased synthesis and is more prevalent than the congenital form. In rare instances, individuals with acquired FXIII deficiency may generate autoantibodies targeting FXIII subunits. Factor XI deficiency (Option B) and Factor XII deficiency (Option D) causes prolonged Activated partial prothrombin time (aPTT) but Prothrombin time (PT) will be normal. Factor X deficiency (Option C) causes both prolonged Prothrombin time (PT) and Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following indicates the primary failure of recovery in an admitted patient with severe acute malnutrition? A. Failure to regain appetite by day 4 B. Failure to start to lose edema by day 4 C. Presence of edema by day 10 D. Weight gain of less than 5gm/kg/day from day 20
questions.stemHtml:
Which of the following indicates the primary failure of recovery in an admitted patient with severe acute malnutrition?
A. Failure to regain appetite by day 4
B. Failure to start to lose edema by day 4
C. Presence of edema by day 10
D. Weight gain of less than 5gm/kg/day from day 20
questions.solution: In an admitted patient with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), primary failure to respond is indicated by the following: Failure to regain appetite by day 4 (Point A) Failure to start to lose edema by day 4 (Point B) If edema still present on day 10 (Point C) Weight gain of less than 5gm/kg/day from day 10, not from day 20 (Point D) (Option B, C and D) Day of admission is counted as day 0 Learning Objective: SAM- Nutritional Rehabilitation Phase and Discharge Nutritional Rehabilitation Entry to Rehabilitation Phase: Indicated by reduced or minimal oedema and a return of appetite. Transition Process: Duration: Over 3 days to prevent refeeding syndrome. Method: Replace F75 with an equal volume of F100 for 2 days. Gradual Increase: Increase feed volume by 10 mL at each feeding until some feed remains uneaten (around 200 mL/kg/day). Post-Transition Feeding: Feeds: Provide unlimited amounts of high-energy, high-protein milk formula like F100 (100 kcal and 3 g protein per 100 mL), ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF), or modified family foods with similar energy and protein content. (Option C) Calories and Protein: Offer 150-220 kcal/kg/day and 4-6 g protein/kg/day. Supplements: Continue potassium, magnesium, and micronutrients. Add iron at 3 mg/kg/day. Breastfeeding: Encourage continued breastfeeding if applicable. RUTF Standard ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) usually contains milk powder, sugar, peanut butter, vegetable oil, vitamins, and minerals. It has a long shelf life and low moisture content- preventing the growth of pathogens. When using RUTF: Begin with small, frequent meals of RUTF, aiming for 8 meals per day initially and then reducing to 5–6 meals per day. If the child cannot consume the full RUTF portion at each meal, supplement with F-75 to complete the meal until they can eat the full amount of RUTF. If the child is unable to consume at least half of the recommended RUTF amount within 12 hours, discontinue RUTF and provide F-75 instead. Reintroduce RUTF after 1–2 days and continue this approach until the child can consume sufficient RUTF. If the child is still breastfeeding, offer breast milk before each RUTF feeding. Discharge criteria All medical issues, including oedema, are resolved for 2 weeks They have completed parenteral antibiotic treatment and the infant is clinically stable and alert. The infant is either breastfeeding effectively or feeding well. The weight gain is satisfactory, such as being above the median of WHO growth velocity standards or gaining more than 5g/kg/day for at least 3 consecutive days. Before discharge, check and provide any missing vaccinations and routine interventions as needed. Ensure that mothers or caregivers are connected with appropriate community follow-up and support. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
In an admitted patient with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), primary failure to respond is indicated by the following:
  • Failure to regain appetite by day 4 (Point A)
  • Failure to start to lose edema by day 4 (Point B)
  • If edema still present on day 10 (Point C)
  • Weight gain of less than 5gm/kg/day from day 10, not from day 20 (Point D) (Option B, C and D)

Day of admission is counted as day 0

 

Learning Objective:
 

SAM- Nutritional Rehabilitation Phase and Discharge

Nutritional Rehabilitation

Entry to Rehabilitation Phase:

  • Indicated by reduced or minimal oedema and a return of appetite.

Transition Process:

  • Duration: Over 3 days to prevent refeeding syndrome.
  • Method: Replace F75 with an equal volume of F100 for 2 days.
  • Gradual Increase: Increase feed volume by 10 mL at each feeding until some feed remains uneaten (around 200 mL/kg/day).

Post-Transition Feeding:

  • Feeds: Provide unlimited amounts of high-energy, high-protein milk formula like F100 (100 kcal and 3 g protein per 100 mL), ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF), or modified family foods with similar energy and protein content. (Option C)
  • Calories and Protein: Offer 150-220 kcal/kg/day and 4-6 g protein/kg/day.
  • Supplements: Continue potassium, magnesium, and micronutrients. Add iron at 3 mg/kg/day.
  • Breastfeeding: Encourage continued breastfeeding if applicable.

RUTF
  • Standard ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) usually contains milk powder, sugar, peanut butter, vegetable oil, vitamins, and minerals.
  • It has a long shelf life and low moisture content- preventing the growth of pathogens.

When using RUTF:

  • Begin with small, frequent meals of RUTF, aiming for 8 meals per day initially and then reducing to 5–6 meals per day. If the child cannot consume the full RUTF portion at each meal, supplement with F-75 to complete the meal until they can eat the full amount of RUTF.
  • If the child is unable to consume at least half of the recommended RUTF amount within 12 hours, discontinue RUTF and provide F-75 instead. Reintroduce RUTF after 1–2 days and continue this approach until the child can consume sufficient RUTF.
  • If the child is still breastfeeding, offer breast milk before each RUTF feeding.

Discharge criteria
  • All medical issues, including oedema, are resolved for 2 weeks
  • They have completed parenteral antibiotic treatment and the infant is clinically stable and alert.
  • The infant is either breastfeeding effectively or feeding well.
  • The weight gain is satisfactory, such as being above the median of WHO growth velocity standards or gaining more than 5g/kg/day for at least 3 consecutive days.
  • Before discharge, check and provide any missing vaccinations and routine interventions as needed. Ensure that mothers or caregivers are connected with appropriate community follow-up and support.

questions.stem: Early-onset pre-eclampsia is defined as pre-eclampsia occurring before which gestational age?
questions.stemHtml: Early-onset pre-eclampsia is defined as pre-eclampsia occurring before which gestational age?
questions.solution: y-onset pre-eclampsia is defined as pre-eclampsia that occurs before 34 weeks of gestation. Preeclampsia: Types of Preeclampsia: Early-Onset Preeclampsia: Occurs at <34 weeks gestation. Etiology: Defective placenta due to altered trophoblast invasion and placental ischemia. Features: Placental infarcts, arterial sclerosis, and hypoperfusion. Late-Onset Preeclampsia: Occurs at ≥34 weeks gestation. Etiology: Healthy placenta interacting with maternal factors, causing microvascular damage and endothelial dysfunction. Features: Maintained placental perfusion; managed expectantly until 37 weeks if stable. Clinical Presentations: New-onset headache unresponsive to medication. Visual disturbances. Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, often with nausea or vomiting. Shortness of breath. Worsened swelling beyond baseline pregnancy-related symptoms. Physical Findings: Elevated blood pressure: SBP ≥140 mmHg or DBP ≥90 mmHg on two measurements at least 4 hours apart. Severe hypertension: SBP ≥160 mmHg or DBP ≥110 mmHg. Edema: Dependent (lower extremities) or independent (face, hands). Lung examination for pulmonary disturbances. Tenderness in the right upper quadrant or epigastric area. Laboratory Tests: Proteinuria: Urine dipstick ≥2+, 24-hour collection ≥300 mg, or protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3. Thrombocytopenia: Platelet count <100 K/mm³. Impaired Liver Function: Liver enzymes >2 times the upper limit of normal. Renal Insufficiency: Serum creatinine ≥1.1 mg/dL or double baseline levels. Management: Antihypertensive Therapy: For severe hypertension (SBP ≥160 mmHg or DBP ≥110 mmHg): IV Medications: Labetalol, hydralazine. Oral Medications: Immediate-release nifedipine. For maintenance: PO Medications: Labetalol, extended-release nifedipine, or clonidine. Seizure Prophylaxis: First-Line: IV magnesium sulfate. Alternatives (if contraindicated): Levetiracetam or benzodiazepines for seizure treatment. Definitive Treatment: Delivery of the fetus is the only definitive cure. Delivery Timing: Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia without Severe Features: Deliver at 37 weeks. Severe Features at ≥34 weeks: Delivery after maternal stabilization. Severe Features <34 weeks: Expectant management with close monitoring and antenatal steroids for fetal lung maturation if stable. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
y-onset pre-eclampsia is defined as pre-eclampsia that occurs before 34 weeks of gestation.
 

Preeclampsia:

  • Types of Preeclampsia:
    • Early-Onset Preeclampsia:
      • Occurs at <34 weeks gestation.
      • Etiology: Defective placenta due to altered trophoblast invasion and placental ischemia.
      • Features: Placental infarcts, arterial sclerosis, and hypoperfusion.
    • Late-Onset Preeclampsia:
  • Occurs at ≥34 weeks gestation.
  • Etiology: Healthy placenta interacting with maternal factors, causing microvascular damage and endothelial dysfunction.
  • Features: Maintained placental perfusion; managed expectantly until 37 weeks if stable.
  • Clinical Presentations:
    • New-onset headache unresponsive to medication.
    • Visual disturbances.
    • Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, often with nausea or vomiting.
    • Shortness of breath.
    • Worsened swelling beyond baseline pregnancy-related symptoms.
  • Physical Findings:
    • Elevated blood pressure:
      • SBP ≥140 mmHg or DBP ≥90 mmHg on two measurements at least 4 hours apart.
      • Severe hypertension: SBP ≥160 mmHg or DBP ≥110 mmHg.
    • Edema: Dependent (lower extremities) or independent (face, hands).
    • Lung examination for pulmonary disturbances.
    • Tenderness in the right upper quadrant or epigastric area.
  • Laboratory Tests:
  • Proteinuria: Urine dipstick ≥2+, 24-hour collection ≥300 mg, or protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3.
  • Thrombocytopenia: Platelet count <100 K/mm³.
  • Impaired Liver Function: Liver enzymes >2 times the upper limit of normal.
  • Renal Insufficiency: Serum creatinine ≥1.1 mg/dL or double baseline levels.
  • Management:
    • Antihypertensive Therapy:
      • For severe hypertension (SBP ≥160 mmHg or DBP ≥110 mmHg):
  • IV Medications: Labetalol, hydralazine.
  • Oral Medications: Immediate-release nifedipine.
  • For maintenance:
    • PO Medications: Labetalol, extended-release nifedipine, or clonidine.
  • Seizure Prophylaxis:
    • First-Line: IV magnesium sulfate.
    • Alternatives (if contraindicated): Levetiracetam or benzodiazepines for seizure treatment.
  • Definitive Treatment: Delivery of the fetus is the only definitive cure.
  • Delivery Timing:
    • Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia without Severe Features: Deliver at 37 weeks.
    • Severe Features at ≥34 weeks: Delivery after maternal stabilization.
    • Severe Features <34 weeks: Expectant management with close monitoring and antenatal steroids for fetal lung maturation if stable.

questions.stem: Dr. Priya is conducting a talk on the screening of cervical cancer with a Pap smear. She works in a clinic in a low-resource setting, and she was planning to screen a woman in her 20s. Which of the following is true regarding cervical cancer screening guidelines in her workplace?
questions.stemHtml: Dr. Priya is conducting a talk on the screening of cervical cancer with a Pap smear. She works in a clinic in a low-resource setting, and she was planning to screen a woman in her 20s. Which of the following is true regarding cervical cancer screening guidelines in her workplace?

options.label: A
options.text: Co-testing (pap and Hr HPV) every 5 years starting at 25 years

options.label: B
options.text: Pap smear every 3 years, starting at 21 years

options.label: C
options.text: Hr HPV testing every 5 years starting at 30 years

options.label: D
options.text: Pap smear every 5 years starting at 21 years

questions.answerText: Pap smear every 3 years, starting at 21 years
questions.solution: data-dictid="6777533153169277719804fcbbf2d1">smear at age 21 and repeating it every 3 years in a low-resource setting. ACOG Protocol for Cervical Cancer Screening: Population Recommendation Aged less than 21 years No screening Aged 21-29 years Cytology alone every 3 years Aged 30-65 years Any one of the following: Cytology alone every 3 years FDA-approved primary hrHPV testing alone every 5 years Cotesting (hrHPV testing and cytology) every 5 years Aged greater than 65 years No screening after adequate negative prior screening results Hysterectomy with removal of the cervix No screening in individuals without a history of high-grade cervical precancerous lesions or cervical cancer WHO Cervical Cancer Screening Guidelines: Population Strategy Screening Test Starting Age Screening Interval General population of women Screen and Treat or Screen, Triage and Treat HPV DNA as primary test 30 years Every 5 to 10 years Women living with HIV Screen, Triage, and Treat only HPV DNA as primary test 25 years Every 3 to 5 years Co-testing (Pap and Hr HPV) every 5 years starting at 25 years (Option A) is recommended for women aged 25 and older, typically in higher-resource settings where both Pap smear and HPV testing are accessible. Hr HPV testing every 5 years starting at 30 years (Option C) is recommended for women aged 30 and older, as younger women tend to clear HPV infections on their own and are less likely to develop cervical cancer from HPV. Pap smear every 5 years starting at 21 years (Option D) is not standard; Pap smears are typically done every 3 years starting at age 21 according to most guidelines. @Neet_pg_bot

Co-testing (Pap and Hr HPV) every 5 years starting at 25 years (Option A) is recommended for women aged 25 and older, typically in higher-resource settings where both Pap smear and HPV testing are accessible.
 

Hr HPV testing every 5 years starting at 30 years (Option C) is recommended for women aged 30 and older, as younger women tend to clear HPV infections on their own and are less likely to develop cervical cancer from HPV.
 

Pap smear every 5 years starting at 21 years (Option D) is not standard; Pap smears are typically done every 3 years starting at age 21 according to most guidelines.

questions.stem: 26-year-old P1L1 presents with abdominal pain. She has a past history of rheumatic heart disease for which she has undergone mitral valve replacement surgery and is on the oral tablet Warfarin 3mg OD. On examination, 14 weeks of abdominal mass were felt. On USG, an 8 X 6 cm unilocular cyst with a reticular pattern was observed in the left ovary. What is the next line of management?
questions.stemHtml: 26-year-old P1L1 presents with abdominal pain. She has a past history of rheumatic heart disease for which she has undergone mitral valve replacement surgery and is on the oral tablet Warfarin 3mg OD. On examination, 14 weeks of abdominal mass were felt. On USG, an 8 X 6 cm unilocular cyst with a reticular pattern was observed in the left ovary. What is the next line of management?
questions.solution: lass="customMeta" data-dictid="1665a40f1016927771801899eaed5d">abdominal pain, a history of mitral valve replacement, and an ovarian cyst with a reticular pattern on ultrasound, suggesting a benign ovarian cyst. The next line of management is to repeat USG after 6-12 weeks to monitor for any changes, as many unilocular cysts resolve spontaneously. Functional Ovarian Cysts: Arise from ovarian follicles during follicle maturation and ovulation. Types: Single Cysts: Most common, often a single follicular or corpus luteum cyst. Multiple Cysts: Can occur in conditions like: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) FSH-secreting pituitary adenomas Features: Functional cysts are typically 3–7 cm, and those larger than 10 cm or persistent for more than 3 months may require further investigation for malignancy. Related to hormonal variations. Filled with clear fluid (unless hemorrhage occurs). Benign, often asymptomatic Typically resolve on their own Management: Observation: Most cysts resolve spontaneously within 4-6 months. Follow-up: Regular ultrasound after 6-12 weeks to monitor persistent or enlarging cysts. Symptomatic Treatment: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) may be prescribed for pain or irregular menses. Surgery: Indicated for cysts larger than 10 cm, persistent, or symptomatic (e.g., pain, torsion). Measure CA 125 levels (Option A): Elevated CA 125 can indicate ovarian cancer but is often raised in benign conditions like menstruation, endometriosis, or pelvic inflammatory disease. It is primarily useful in postmenopausal women with suspected malignancy. Surgical intervention (Option C): Immediate surgery is unnecessary for a simple ovarian cyst. Surgery is typically considered if the cyst persists, grows, or causes acute symptoms like torsion or rupture. MRI pelvis (Option D): Transvaginal ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality for ovarian cysts. MRI is typically used for complex or uncertain cases, which is not necessary here. @Neet_pg_bot

lass="customMeta" data-dictid="1665a40f1016927771801899eaed5d">abdominal pain, a history of mitral valve replacement, and an ovarian cyst with a reticular pattern on ultrasound, suggesting a benign ovarian cyst. The next line of management is to repeat USG after 6-12 weeks to monitor for any changes, as many unilocular cysts resolve spontaneously.
 

Functional Ovarian Cysts:

  • Arise from ovarian follicles during follicle maturation and ovulation.
  • Types:
    • Single Cysts: Most common, often a single follicular or corpus luteum cyst.
    • Multiple Cysts: Can occur in conditions like:
      • Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
      • Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS)
      • FSH-secreting pituitary adenomas
  • Features:
    • Functional cysts are typically 3–7 cm, and those larger than 10 cm or persistent for more than 3 months may require further investigation for malignancy.
    • Related to hormonal variations.
    • Filled with clear fluid (unless hemorrhage occurs).
    • Benign, often asymptomatic
    • Typically resolve on their own
  • Management:
    • Observation: Most cysts resolve spontaneously within 4-6 months.
      • Follow-up: Regular ultrasound after 6-12 weeks to monitor persistent or enlarging cysts.
      • Symptomatic Treatment: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) may be prescribed for pain or irregular menses.
      • Surgery: Indicated for cysts larger than 10 cm, persistent, or symptomatic (e.g., pain, torsion).
         

Measure CA 125 levels (Option A): Elevated CA 125 can indicate ovarian cancer but is often raised in benign conditions like menstruation, endometriosis, or pelvic inflammatory disease. It is primarily useful in postmenopausal women with suspected malignancy.

Surgical intervention (Option C): Immediate surgery is unnecessary for a simple ovarian cyst. Surgery is typically considered if the cyst persists, grows, or causes acute symptoms like torsion or rupture.


MRI pelvis (Option D): Transvaginal ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality for ovarian cysts. MRI is typically used for complex or uncertain cases, which is not necessary here.

questions.stemHtml: When is delayed cord clamping recommended?

options.label: A
options.text: Term and preterm babies, irrespective of birth weights

options.label: B
options.text: Vigorous term and preterm babies requiring resuscitation

options.label: C
options.text: Vigorous term babies not requiring resuscitation

options.label: D
options.text: All term babies born at 37 weeks

questions.answerText: Term and preterm babies, irrespective of birth weights
questions.solution: Meta" data-dictid="ac9f7287191692777196e8c02d1f3d">preterm babies, irrespective of birth weight. Delayed Umbilical Cord Clamping: Timing Recommended delay: At least 30-60 seconds after birth for vigorous term and preterm infants (per ACOG). Benefits for Term Infants Increased Hemoglobin Levels: Higher levels at birth. Improved Iron Stores: Better reserves during the first several months of life. Positive Developmental Impact: Potential improvement in neurodevelopmental outcomes. Benefits for Preterm Infants Improved Circulation: Enhanced transitional circulation to support physiological adaptation. Higher RBC Volume: Better blood volume establishment. Reduced Complications: Lower rates of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Reduced incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). Decreased Need for Blood Transfusions: Fewer transfusions required in neonatal care. Maternal Safety No significant increase in postpartum hemorrhage or blood loss. No differences in postpartum hemoglobin levels or the need for maternal transfusion. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Meta" data-dictid="ac9f7287191692777196e8c02d1f3d">preterm babies, irrespective of birth weight.

Delayed Umbilical Cord Clamping:

 

Timing

Recommended delay: At least 30-60 seconds after birth for vigorous term and preterm infants (per ACOG).

Benefits for Term Infants
  • Increased Hemoglobin Levels: Higher levels at birth.
  • Improved Iron Stores: Better reserves during the first several months of life.
  • Positive Developmental Impact: Potential improvement in neurodevelopmental outcomes.

Benefits for Preterm Infants
  • Improved Circulation: Enhanced transitional circulation to support physiological adaptation.
  • Higher RBC Volume: Better blood volume establishment.
  • Reduced Complications:
    • Lower rates of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC).
    • Reduced incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH).
  • Decreased Need for Blood Transfusions: Fewer transfusions required in neonatal care.

Maternal Safety
  • No significant increase in postpartum hemorrhage or blood loss.
  • No differences in postpartum hemoglobin levels or the need for maternal transfusion.

questions.stem: A couple presents with infertility even after 2 years of unprotected intercourse. The seminal analysis reveals a volume of 2 ml, concentration of 40 million/ml, progressive motility of 55%, and morphology of 45 %. The wife's hormone levels were normal, with bilateral spillage of dye from both fallopian tubes on HSG. What percentage of couples can be attributed to unexplained infertility?

The wife's hormone levels were normal, with bilateral spillage of dye from both fallopian tubes on HSG. What percentage of couples can be attributed to unexplained infertility?
questions.solution: pan> analysis, ovulation, and tubal patency, suggesting unexplained infertility in approximately 25% of such cases. Unexplained infertility refers to infertile couples with normal ovulation, tubal patency, and semen analysis. Its prevalence ranges from 22-28%. Semen Analysis and Normal Values: First investigation for infertility in males. Performed after 1 year of unprotected intercourse without conception or earlier if there are known risk factors for infertility. Abstain: 2-7 days. Analysis: Within 1 hour on the liquefied semen (takes 20-30 min). Parameters Normal (Normozoospermia) (WHO 2021 Guidelines) Volume > 1.4 ml pH 7.2-8.0 Concentration At least 16 million/ ml Total count 39 million/ejaculate Total Motility 42% or more Progressive motility 30% or more Morphology (most important) 4% or more Pus cells (WBC) 1-2 million/ml Viability 54% or more Note: Oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OATZ) means all parameters are subnormal, as seen in varicocele and smoking. The most important parameters in sperm analysis are Morphology > Motility > Concentration. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Abstain: 2-7 days.
  • Analysis: Within 1 hour on the liquefied semen (takes 20-30 min).

 

Parameters

Normal (Normozoospermia)

(WHO 2021 Guidelines)

Volume

> 1.4 ml

pH

7.2-8.0

Concentration

At least 16 million/ ml

Total count

39 million/ejaculate

Total Motility

42% or more

Progressive motility

30% or more

Morphology (most important)

4% or more

1-2 million/ml

54% or more

 

Note:

  • Oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OATZ) means all parameters are subnormal, as seen in varicocele and smoking.

options.label: A

questions.answerText: Increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks
questions.solution: > Explanation: In pregnancy, an increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks is not a physiological change. Blood Pressure in Pregnancy: Declines early in pregnancy, reaching a nadir at 24-26 weeks; diastolic pressure decreases more than systolic. Positional Changes: BP is lower in lateral positions compared to sitting or supine positions. Supine Hypotensive Syndrome: Uterus compresses great vessels, causing significant hypotension in some women. Blood Volume in Pregnancy: Hypervolemia: Blood volume increases by 40-45% above nonpregnant levels by 32-34 weeks of gestation. In some cases, blood volume nearly doubles. Plasma and Erythrocyte Mass: Plasma volume increases more than erythrocyte mass. Erythrocyte volume increases by ~450 mL due to moderate bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia and elevated plasma erythropoietin levels. (Option D) Hemoglobin and Hematocrit: Hemoglobin concentration decreases slightly, averaging 12.5 g/dL at term. Metabolic Changes in Pregnancy: Glucose Levels: Characterized by mild fasting hypoglycemia, postprandial hyperglycemia, and hyperinsulinemia. (Option B) Insulin Sensitivity: Reduced by 30-70% in late pregnancy due to: Hormones: Progesterone, cortisol, placentally derived growth hormone, and prolactin. Cytokines: Tumor necrosis factor and leptin. Postprandial Glucose: Elevated due to insulin resistance and augmented hepatic gluconeogenesis. Fasting State: (OptionC) Lower glucose and amino acids. >
Explanation:

In pregnancy, an increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after 6 weeks is not a physiological change.
 

Blood Pressure in Pregnancy:

  • Declines early in pregnancy, reaching a nadir at 24-26 weeks; diastolic pressure decreases more than systolic.
  • Positional Changes: BP is lower in lateral positions compared to sitting or supine positions.
  • Supine Hypotensive Syndrome: Uterus compresses great vessels, causing significant hypotension in some women.

 

Blood Volume in Pregnancy:

  • Hypervolemia: Blood volume increases by 40-45% above nonpregnant levels by 32-34 weeks of gestation. In some cases, blood volume nearly doubles.
  • Plasma and Erythrocyte Mass:
    • Plasma volume increases more than erythrocyte mass.
    • Erythrocyte volume increases by ~450 mL due to moderate bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia and elevated plasma erythropoietin levels. (Option D)
  • Hemoglobin and Hematocrit: Hemoglobin concentration decreases slightly, averaging 12.5 g/dL at term.

 

Metabolic Changes in Pregnancy:

  • Glucose Levels: Characterized by mild fasting hypoglycemia, postprandial hyperglycemia, and hyperinsulinemia. (Option B)
  • Insulin Sensitivity: Reduced by 30-70% in late pregnancy due to:
    • Hormones: Progesterone, cortisol, placentally derived growth hormone, and prolactin.
    • Cytokines: Tumor necrosis factor and leptin.
  • Postprandial Glucose: Elevated due to insulin resistance and augmented hepatic gluconeogenesis.
  • Fasting State: (OptionC)
    • Lower glucose and amino acids.
    • Higher free fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol.
    • Ketonemia develops rapidly during prolonged fasting.

questions.stemHtml: In the context of labor and delivery, what does "restitution" refer to?

options.label: A
options.text: Passive movement of head due to untwisting of neck

options.label: B
options.text: Movement of the head by 1/8th of the circle due to torsion

options.label: C
options.text: Stretching of the vulval outlet by the head

options.label: D
options.text: External rotation after delivery of shoulder

questions.answerText: Passive movement of head due to untwisting of neck
questions.solution: rong> Restitution is the passive movement of head due to untwisting of neck. Restitution: It is the repositioning of the fetal head attitude immediately after delivery, returning it to normal alignment with the body. It involves visible external movement of the fetal head to correct the torsion of the neck sustained during internal rotation. The direction of this movement is opposite to that of internal rotation (45°). This movement allows the head to align with the shoulders, with the occiput pointing towards the maternal thigh of the corresponding side where it originally lies. As restitution occurs, the fetal head reaches a transverse position, and the fetal body aligns its bisacromial diameter (the distance across the shoulders) with the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet. As a result, one shoulder moves anteriorly, positioning behind the symphysis, while the other shoulder moves posteriorly. @Neet_pg_bot

  • As restitution occurs, the fetal head reaches a transverse position, and the fetal body aligns its bisacromial diameter (the distance across the shoulders) with the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of AMTSL?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is NOT part of AMTSL?

options.label: B
options.text: Delivery of placenta by controlled cord traction

options.label: D
options.text: Administration of oxytocin after shoulder delivery

questions.solution: trong>Explanation: Bimanual compression is not a part of AMTSL. Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL): AMTSL is a set of practices aimed at enhancing uterine contractions to facilitate placental delivery and prevent primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). Key Steps: Administration of Uterotonic Medication: (Option D) A uterotonic drug, such as oxytocin, is administered within one minute of the baby's birth or immediately after the delivery of the anterior shoulder. Significance : This is the most critical step in promoting uterine contractions and reducing bleeding. Delayed Cord Clamping: The umbilical cord is clamped and cut 1–3 minutes after the baby is delivered. Purpose : Optimizes neonatal blood volume and reduces the risk of anemia. Controlled Cord Traction (CCT): (Option B) The placenta is delivered using a modified technique ( Brandt-Andrews method ), involving gentle pulling on the cord while supporting the uterus. Benefit : Helps prevent uterine inversion and ensures safe placental delivery. Assessment of Uterine Tone : Intermittently check the uterine fundus to confirm adequate tone and contractility. Routine uterine massage (Option A) is no longer universally recommended but may be performed if needed. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>Explanation:

Bimanual compression is not a part of AMTSL.
 

Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL):

  • AMTSL is a set of practices aimed at enhancing uterine contractions to facilitate placental delivery and prevent primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH).
  • Key Steps:
    • Administration of Uterotonic Medication: (Option D)
  • A uterotonic drug, such as oxytocin, is administered within one minute of the baby's birth or immediately after the delivery of the anterior shoulder.
  • Significance: This is the most critical step in promoting uterine contractions and reducing bleeding.
  • Delayed Cord Clamping:
    • The umbilical cord is clamped and cut 1–3 minutes after the baby is delivered.
    • Purpose: Optimizes neonatal blood volume and reduces the risk of anemia.
  • Controlled Cord Traction (CCT): (Option B)
    • The placenta is delivered using a modified technique (Brandt-Andrews method), involving gentle pulling on the cord while supporting the uterus.
    • Benefit: Helps prevent uterine inversion and ensures safe placental delivery.
  • Assessment of Uterine Tone:
    • Intermittently check the uterine fundus to confirm adequate tone and contractility.
    • Routine uterine massage (Option A) is no longer universally recommended but may be performed if needed.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old P2L2 woman presents with malodorous vaginal discharge and a normal cervix. The whiff test is positive. What is this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old P2L2 woman presents with malodorous vaginal discharge and a normal cervix. The whiff test is positive. What is this condition?
questions.solution: lodorous discharge in the female is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis. Bacterial Vaginosis (BV): A polymicrobial condition characterized by an alteration in normal vaginal flora. Minimal inflammatory response; few leukocytes in vaginal fluid. Pathogenesis: Decreased lactobacilli, leading to increased pH and overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria. Common bacteria: Gardnerella vaginalis, Mobiluncus spp., Mycoplasma hominis, and Haemophilus vaginalis. Not sexually transmitted. Symptoms: 50% are asymptomatic. Vaginal discharge: white, milky, non-viscous, and adherent. Minimal vulval irritation. Amsel's Criteria (Diagnostic Features): White, milky, nonviscous discharge adherent to the vaginal wall. Discharge with pH >4.5. Fishy odor on adding 10% KOH ( whiff test ). Presence of clue cells on wet mount. Reduced lactobacilli and increased pathogenic bacteria. Complications: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) Chorioamnionitis Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) Preterm labor Treatment: Metronidazole (DOC): 400 mg twice daily for 7 days (effective in 85%). A single 1 g dose cures only 45%. Clindamycin: 2% cream locally (85% effective). Oral 300 mg daily for 7 days. Alternatives: Ampicillin, cephalosporin, tetracycline, doxycycline, or sulfa drugs. Candida (Option A) causes thick, white, cottage cheese-like discharge, itching, and presents with pseudohyphae and yeast cells on KOH mount, but not a fishy odor or positive whiff test. Trichomonas vaginalis (Option C) causes frothy, greenish-yellow discharge with itching, burning, and motile trichomonas on wet mount, but lacks a fishy odor and positive whiff test. Physiological cause (Option D) results in clear, odorless discharge that varies with the menstrual cycle and does not have a fishy odor or a positive whiff test. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
lodorous discharge in the female is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.

Bacterial Vaginosis (BV):
  • A polymicrobial condition characterized by an alteration in normal vaginal flora.
  • Minimal inflammatory response; few leukocytes in vaginal fluid.
  • Pathogenesis:
  • Decreased lactobacilli, leading to increased pH and overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria.
  • Common bacteria: Gardnerella vaginalis, Mobiluncus spp., Mycoplasma hominis, and Haemophilus vaginalis.
  • Not sexually transmitted.
  • Symptoms:
  • 50% are asymptomatic.
  • Vaginal discharge: white, milky, non-viscous, and adherent.
  • Minimal vulval irritation.
  • Amsel's Criteria (Diagnostic Features):
  • White, milky, nonviscous discharge adherent to the vaginal wall.
  • Discharge with pH >4.5.
  • Fishy odor on adding 10% KOH (whiff test).
  • Presence of clue cells on wet mount.

  • Reduced lactobacilli and increased pathogenic bacteria.
  • Complications:
    • Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
    • Chorioamnionitis
    • Premature rupture of membranes (PROM)
    • Preterm labor
  • Treatment:
  • Metronidazole (DOC):
    • 400 mg twice daily for 7 days (effective in 85%).
    • A single 1 g dose cures only 45%.
  • Clindamycin:
    • 2% cream locally (85% effective).
    • Oral 300 mg daily for 7 days.
  • Alternatives:
    • Ampicillin, cephalosporin, tetracycline, doxycycline, or sulfa drugs.

 

Candida (Option A) causes thick, white, cottage cheese-like discharge, itching, and presents with pseudohyphae and yeast cells on KOH mount, but not a fishy odor or positive whiff test.

 

Trichomonas vaginalis (Option C) causes frothy, greenish-yellow discharge with itching, burning, and motile trichomonas on wet mount, but lacks a fishy odor and positive whiff test.

 

Physiological cause (Option D) results in clear, odorless discharge that varies with the menstrual cycle and does not have a fishy odor or a positive whiff test.

questions.stemHtml: An athlete with a BMI of 17.5 kg/m2 presents with secondary amenorrhea and primary infertility. Her laboratory investigations reveal FSH 2, LH 0.3, and TSH 1.2. Prolactin 20ng/ml. What is the underlying cause of this condition?
questions.solution: ta" data-dictid="02315055441692777203a721dd9b19">FSH and LH levels with a history of low BMI in an athlete indicate reduced GnRH production, consistent with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (HH): It results from hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction, leading to inadequate gonadotropin secretion. Classification: Congenital HH: Anosmic HH (e.g., Kallmann syndrome): Associated with impaired or absent sense of smell; MRI may show absent or abnormal olfactory bulbs. Congenital Normosmic Isolated HH: Normal sense of smell. Acquired HH: May result from tumors, trauma, weight loss, excessive exercise , stress, systemic illness, or medications. Clinical Characteristics: Androgen deficiency: Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, muscle weakness, and increased adiposity. Impaired or delayed pubertal sexual maturation. Depressed mood, decreased vitality, reduced bone density, and infertility. Diagnosis: Low testosterone and low levels of pituitary hormones (LH and FSH). Low serum levels of estradiol. Stimulated intravenous GnRH test may help confirm the diagnosis. MRI for anosmic HH may reveal anomalies in olfactory structures. Management: Hormonal Therapy: Used to stimulate sexual development and regularize menstrual cycles in cases of congenital HH. Cause-Specific Therapy: Targeted treatment for acquired causes based on the underlying condition. Fertility Treatment: Ovulation induction using GnRH or gonadotropins. Primary ovarian failure (Option A) is marked by irregular or absent menstrual cycles, with elevated FSH and decreased estradiol levels indicating a primary ovarian defect. This condition typically results in sterility, which does not align with the patient’s suppressed FSH and LH levels in this case. Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism (Option C) is associated with ovarian failure leading to high FSH and LH due to a lack of negative feedback from the ovaries. It is not relevant here as the patient’s gonadotropin levels are suppressed, not elevated. Normogonadotropic Normogonadism (Option D) implies normal hypothalamic-pituitary function, with FSH and LH levels in the normal range. Amenorrhea in such cases is often due to PCOS or other structural or systemic causes, none of which align with the suppressed gonadotropins seen in this patient. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ta" data-dictid="02315055441692777203a721dd9b19">FSH and LH levels with a history of low BMI in an athlete indicate reduced GnRH production, consistent with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
 

Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (HH):

  • It results from hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction, leading to inadequate gonadotropin secretion.
  • Classification:
    • Congenital HH:
      • Anosmic HH (e.g., Kallmann syndrome): Associated with impaired or absent sense of smell; MRI may show absent or abnormal olfactory bulbs.
      • Congenital Normosmic Isolated HH: Normal sense of smell.
    • Acquired HH: May result from tumors, trauma, weight loss, excessive exercise, stress, systemic illness, or medications.
  • Clinical Characteristics:
    • Androgen deficiency: Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, muscle weakness, and increased adiposity.
    • Impaired or delayed pubertal sexual maturation.
    • Depressed mood, decreased vitality, reduced bone density, and infertility.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Low testosterone and low levels of pituitary hormones (LH and FSH).
    • Low serum levels of estradiol.
    • Stimulated intravenous GnRH test may help confirm the diagnosis.
    • MRI for anosmic HH may reveal anomalies in olfactory structures.
  • Management:
    • Hormonal Therapy: Used to stimulate sexual development and regularize menstrual cycles in cases of congenital HH.
    • Cause-Specific Therapy: Targeted treatment for acquired causes based on the underlying condition.
    • Fertility Treatment: Ovulation induction using GnRH or gonadotropins.

 

Primary ovarian failure (Option A) is marked by irregular or absent menstrual cycles, with elevated FSH and decreased estradiol levels indicating a primary ovarian defect. This condition typically results in sterility, which does not align with the patient’s suppressed FSH and LH levels in this case.

 

Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism (Option C) is associated with ovarian failure leading to high FSH and LH due to a lack of negative feedback from the ovaries. It is not relevant here as the patient’s gonadotropin levels are suppressed, not elevated.

 

Normogonadotropic Normogonadism (Option D) implies normal hypothalamic-pituitary function, with FSH and LH levels in the normal range. Amenorrhea in such cases is often due to PCOS or other structural or systemic causes, none of which align with the suppressed gonadotropins seen in this patient.
